# Default Configuration and Shadow Tree Decision Record

When Capture Pipeline 2.4 was drafted, the default configuration contract and shadow DOM descendants were put in the same record. This arrangement only settled where to keep the record: both had come up within the scope of capture, and there was no material at the time to point each one to a more specific implementation entry point.

## 2023-04-19 Drafting Assessment

At that point, there were two ways to organize this.

- Split default configuration and shadow tree descendants into separate records, each awaiting further clarification.
- Keep a shared page, first record that both had come up as issues, and decide later whether to split them.

Selected the second option. The reason was not that the two share a call chain, or that the configuration object contains node snapshots; it was simply that such a relationship could not safely be established at the time. The shared page should retain the open questions, not treat two issues appearing together as a single behavior.

## Investigation Starting Points at the Time

Earlier investigation notes pointed from the issue and call names to `src/js/lib/config.js`. The file header showed:

```js
import T from './tool.js';
```

# Decision Record for Default Configuration and Shadow Trees

This page was initially just a shared landing place for Capture Pipeline 2.4. The default configuration contract and shadow DOM descendants appeared side by side in the earliest records, and people later used them separately to trace the entry point for default configuration and the boundaries of node objects. The page was not rewritten to follow a single track because those traces of how it was used themselves explain several persistent misreadings: why file location was once treated as ownership, why defaults were once reduced to a local fallback, and why slot assignment was for a time treated as another way of referring to shadow tree descendants.

Looking back now, the original shared page was not a complete design, but a decision point that had not yet been split up. The point of retaining it is not to prove that the two objects belong to the same implementation, but to keep the original assumptions visible when later corrections are made. What follows preserves, in order, the wording used during drafting, the points where review paused, the approaches to organizing the material that were abandoned, and the configuration object requirements that have now been finalized.

## 2023-04-19: Why They Were Initially Kept on One Page

The first version made just one very small decision: not to split the page yet. Configuration defaults and shadow tree descendants were both mentioned within the capture scope of 2.4, but there was no material at the time indicating that they shared data structures, call paths, or a fix location. Splitting the page by implementation ownership would require first assuming a particular entry point; immediately placing it under a broader "capture behavior" topic would lose the differences between the two objects that had not yet been clarified.

The choice at the time was therefore to retain a shared heading. This choice settled where to record things, not technical ownership. The original page made no commitment that default configuration controls the shadow tree, nor that snapshots of the shadow tree are produced by the configuration object. It merely allowed later material to be appended in the same place, and required additions to first state whether they concerned the configuration object, the node object, or navigational clues left by earlier investigations.

The draft page took a very cautious tone. Default configuration was described as an object that needed review, while shadow tree descendants were described as an object that needed to be identified. Version fields and capture strategy fields were recorded only as categories that might need checking; shadow DOM descendants, ordinary ordered child nodes, and slot assignment were likewise recorded only as terms that must not be conflated prematurely. There was no field table, no node table, and no use of a catch-all "snapshot processing" label to obscure the differences between the objects.

This early constraint is still worth retaining. It is not a substitute for the rules established later, but it explains why the old page left many gaps: the gaps were due to the lack of direct material at the time, not because the two topics did not need to be explained separately in the first place.

## File Entry Point Recorded on the Same Day

The old investigation notes linked the issue name and call name to `src/js/lib/config.js`. This entry point was the only source code location explicitly preserved at the time. The file header shows:

```js
import T from './tool.js';
import MxWcStorage from './storage.js';
```

The drafter copied the two imports onto the page, so that later reviews could start from the same place. They indicate only that these two direct dependencies exist near the top of the configuration file. The original record did not explain the role of `T`, nor did it explain whether `MxWcStorage` was involved in the default object, capture policy, shadow tree, or slot snapshots; we should not retroactively supply those explanations today either.

This entry-point record later had a side effect. Some people would open this file first, then naturally interpret all the issues on the page as responsibilities of that file. This understanding did not come from an explicitly stated conclusion on the draft page, but it could easily arise from the layout: the path came first, followed by unresolved objects, making them look like implementation gaps in the same place. The later addendum was added to address this misreading.

## 2023-08-31: What the review did not prove

The second revision began by returning to the old path. The review retained only a narrow finding: the earlier investigation did indeed lead readers examining the default configuration to `src/js/lib/config.js`. This was enough to retain the path as a navigation aid, but not enough to establish that the file defined the boundary of all the behavior.

At the time, one tempting inference was not adopted. Since `T` and `MxWcStorage` were visible in the configuration file, it seemed possible to interpret the default configuration, based on the names, as a bridge object between tools and storage; and because the shadow-tree issue appeared alongside capture, it seemed possible to place it within that bridging relationship. This explanation had no direct support in the material, and merely stitched adjacent names, the same version range, and the location of the earlier investigation into a story. The review stopped there, without writing that story up as a decision.

To keep the text that followed from lumping the three types of information together again, the second version introduced a simple distinction: a file path is a navigation aid; the default configuration is an object contract; shadow-tree descendants are a matter of node semantics. The three layers can be adjacent, but they answer different questions.

| Record layer | Conclusions that can be retained | Conclusions that cannot simply be added |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Navigation | The earlier investigation reached the configuration file from issue names and call names | The configuration file owns all capture logic |
| Configuration | The object as a whole, the version, and the capture policy need verification | The default configuration is merely a set of scattered fallback values |
| Nodes | Descendants, order, and slot snapshots need to be distinguished | The three ways of describing nodes are equivalent to one another |

This table is not an architecture diagram. It records the leaps that had to be avoided when reading a page of old material at the time. A path can tell people where to look; an object contract must be assessed from the object itself; node scope requires material on nodes. The three did not automatically form a single runtime relationship just because they were written on the same page.

## Where the review left off

During the review in 2023, an attempt was made to split the shared page into two. One would cover only configuration defaults, and the other only shadow DOM descendants. This effort was not completed, not because the split was necessarily wrong, but because the reasons for splitting it at the time were too weak.

If the shadow tree topic were immediately given its own section, readers might assume that it already had independent, stable rules; however, the review left no concrete node samples. If it remained in the configuration chapter, readers might instead assume that node scope belonged to the default object; that would be equally unfounded. Both approaches would prematurely present the boundary as settled.

What remained, then, was not an empty statement of "no decision for now", but a limited decision: retain the shared page, with configuration and nodes documented separately within it. The default configuration section may only discuss whether the object is complete and why version and capture strategy are categories that need to be checked; the shadow tree section may only discuss the fact that the terms for the objects are not interchangeable. Without samples, do not sketch hypothetical results for node relationships; without interface output, do not list hypothetical fields for the configuration object either.

Stopping at this point was once mistaken for a lack of a conclusion. In fact, it put an end to an unreliable way of organizing the material: a visible file entry point does not mean that all adjacent topics can be crammed back into that entry point. The review did not produce a complete specification, but it did rule out the reading that "the entry point equals the boundary", which was the change actually achieved at the time.

## Old approach: Organizing by file location

Retained below is the classification approach used at the time. This text is no longer followed as the current practice.

> First look for default values near the configuration file; if there is no explanation of shadow DOM descendants, treat it as an omitted part of the default configuration and fill the gap in the same place.

This approach had a clear convenience at the time: anyone investigating needed to remember only one file, and the initial notes did not need to decide exactly where the two objects should be separated. For a newly created working page, this consolidation seemed to save a lot of effort.

The problem lay in that same convenience. The approach conflated "file location", "the externally exposed shape of the default configuration", and "the collection semantics of shadow tree nodes". Not seeing an object in the file does not mean that the object is not part of the behavior; seeing several default values in the default configuration does not mean that the object contains only those values; node names and configuration names appearing on the same page is even less reason to conclude that the former are missing items in the latter.

**This passage is obsolete.** Going forward, "whether there is an explanation near the configuration file" will no longer be used to determine whether rules exist for shadow DOM descendants, and node issues will no longer be treated as a missing field in the default object. The original text has not been deleted, because it explains why the old page kept the two topics tied together for so long; deleting this approach would remove the context for the corrections that follow.

Another earlier idea was to classify things in the opposite direction: since capture strategy might affect capture scope, relegate both version and capture strategy to incidental information attached to node snapshots. This idea was not adopted either. When version and capture strategy entered the discussion, they referred to the scope of verification for the configuration object; reducing them to side notes for snapshots would once again let node names subsume the object contract.

## Two side notes from the review

The subsequent review provided neither a complete node design nor all the configuration keys. It left two more specific requirements for interpreting the text.

The first concerns "default configuration". Seeing only one key is not grounds for declaring the object complete; finding only one object entry point is likewise not grounds for declaring that the extension has read every possible key. The review required "the object as a whole" and "individual fields" to be documented separately. This requirement later became a prerequisite for checking version and capture strategy: they are categories of keys that need to be confirmed, not a complete field list invented by the documentation.

The second note concerns how nodes are described. shadow DOM descendants and slot assignment snapshots should not be used as synonyms. The former emphasizes descendant objects in the shadow tree; the latter emphasizes the snapshot context created by slot assignment. They may appear close together in a discussion of a single capture, but they cannot be used interchangeably just because both concern nodes. Ordinary ordered child nodes should also retain their own object name, because ordering itself is a separate point of discussion.

These two marginal notes are lightweight in form, but their content changes how the page is written. Any future addition of shadow-tree material must first make clear whether it discusses descendants, ordered child nodes, or slot assignment. Any future addition of configuration material must first make clear whether it discusses the object as a whole or a particular known key. If these distinctions are skipped, the old categorization will reappear in different wording.

## Old Example 1: Import Names Treated as Responsibility Names

Someone once inferred from `MxWcStorage` at the top of the configuration file that the default configuration must be tied to the save process, and then inferred from `T` that it included shadow-tree handling. This example never became a formal conclusion, but it is worth keeping on the page as a past reading error.

Import relationships can only indicate local adjacency for the current file. Names that appear related do not mean that responsibilities have been explained. In this historical account in particular, configuration objects and node objects are already easy to conflate because they share a page; using import names to fill in responsibilities would disguise missing material as a seemingly natural implementation diagram.

This old example now serves only as a reminder of the reading order: first distinguish whether you are investigating object conventions or node semantics, then decide whether file adjacency can help locate the relevant material. It cannot support any further assertions about storage, tools, or the shadow-tree implementation.

## Old Example 2: Shortening Slot Snapshots to Descendants

In the early text, someone suggested directly using slot assignment snapshots in place of shadow DOM descendants for brevity. This shortened wording was not retained.

Slot assignment snapshots and shadow-tree descendants are not terms for the same object. Even if a single capture process needs to observe both, their differences cannot be erased with the expectation that callers will reconstruct them on their own. If the material only discusses slot assignment, it can only add information about slot snapshots; if it only discusses ordered child nodes, it can only add information about ordering; if it is intended to explain shadow-tree descendants, it must explicitly identify shadow-tree descendants as its scope.

The old example is kept nearby because it reveals another risk of a shared page: compressing multiple objects into one label to make a sentence shorter. The "local default values" misreading in the configuration section and the "snapshot nodes" misreading in the node section actually share the same root cause: reducing objects that have not yet been thoroughly checked to names that make them easy to categorize.

## States Used on the Current Page

For ease of maintenance, this page diagrams only the progression of historical judgments as states, not as a runtime structure. The states in the diagram indicate how a judgment in the documentation is retained, reviewed, or discarded; they do not indicate that the default configuration flows into the shadow tree, nor that the configuration file is responsible for node snapshots.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Shared record
    Shared record --> File entry retained
    Shared record --> Configuration object pending verification
    Shared record --> Node object pending verification
    File entry retained --> Entry is not a boundary
    Configuration object pending verification --> Old notion of local default values deprecated
    Node object pending verification --> Slot snapshot is not an alias
    Entry is not a boundary --> Current layering
    Old notion of local default values deprecated --> Current layering
    Slot snapshot is not an alias --> Current layering
```

The most important step in the diagram is "Entry is not a boundary." It preserves why the old investigation started from `src/js/lib/config.js`, while also removing the interpretation that the path should automatically expand to include all technical ownership. The configuration object and node object continue to exist separately; one entry is no longer required to stand in for the other object when drawing conclusions.

## Cross-cutting issue still not split out

There is another adjacent issue on the page: when the capture strategy changes, do subsequent checks need to inspect the shadow tree, slot assignment, and regular ordered child nodes at the same time? This issue was not removed because it can indeed affect both the configuration side and the node side at the same time.

But for now it is only a cross-cutting issue, not an established causal relationship. One cannot infer from "the strategy may affect the inspection scope" that "the strategy defines all node rules"; nor can one infer from "node rules still need to be supplemented" that "the version and capture strategy are outside the scope of the default configuration." The former error would expand configuration keys into node design, while the latter would reduce object content that already needs confirmation to irrelevant details.

This issue remains on this page rather than being moved to a separate node record so that the original layering can still be found when additional relationship material is added later. Next time, if direct evidence becomes available, first state clearly whether it changes the meaning of the configuration object, the scope of the node object, or adds an explicit relationship between the two. If all that is found is another path name, it should not be used to restart the old approach of narrowing by file location.

## 2025-07-29 Current decision

Following the drafting record, path review, the unfinished split attempt, retirement of the old categorization, and review margin notes, the default-configuration side no longer uses the framing of "a collection of local fallback values." The current decision concerns the public object itself, not the file location, nor the node semantics of the shadow tree:

Config.getDefault exposes the complete baseline configuration object, including the version and capture policy keys used by the extension.
This decision replaces the earlier narrower description with a requirement for the object as a whole. Here, complete refers to the baseline configuration object, not a field catalog invented by this page itself. version and capture policy are categories of keys used by the extension and must be confirmed along with the object contract; finding just one isolated value among them is not enough to mark the default configuration as fully verified.

Therefore, when discussing the default configuration, first treat the baseline object returned by `Config.getDefault` as the unit under review, then confirm version and capture policy. The old file entry point can still be used to reconstruct the investigation history, and the imports at the top of the file can still serve as adjacent reading references, but neither can replace an assessment of this public object. This settles the current requirements for the configuration object, and the old description that it "may just be a few fallback values" is retained only as a historical interpretation.

The current decision does not change the boundaries of the shadow-tree section. It does not include shadow DOM descendants in the definition of the default object, nor does it claim that shadow-tree descendants are directly determined by `Config.getDefault`. Discussion of the shadow tree must still distinguish between descendants, ordinary ordered child nodes, and slot assignment snapshots; what this page has established is that these objects must not be collapsed into the same thing based on configuration file paths or configuration key names.

## Review order following the decision

When the default configuration needs to be confirmed, first check the object contract exposed by `Config.getDefault`. To understand why the old records ended up pointing to the configuration file, then revisit `src/js/lib/config.js` and the visible imports. The first step confirms the current object, and the second reconstructs the historical navigation; do not reverse the order and then infer the object's completeness from the path.

When addressing the shadow-tree topic, first confirm whether the question is about shadow DOM descendants, ordered child nodes, or slot assignment snapshots. Only after the object has been identified can you decide at which layer to add subsequent material. Do not replace all of these descriptions with "node snapshots" just because these terms all appear within the capture scope.

The shared page is still being retained, but the reason now differs from the one in the year 2023: it is no longer because there is no boundary at all between the two topics, but because their shared records, misinterpretations, corrections, and current layering remain visible here as a continuous history. If the page is split in the future, the old proposals, review margin notes, and this decision on the configuration object should be migrated according to their relationships, rather than moving only the final sentence stating the requirement.

## Left for the next review

The following questions have not yet been resolved by this page:

- A direct description of shadow DOM descendants in specific snapshots still needs to be added separately;
- The relationship between slot assignment snapshots and shadow-tree descendants cannot be inferred from the similarity of their names;
- How ordinary ordered child nodes are handled cannot be inferred from the completeness of the default configuration object;
- If a new default configuration entry point appears, its relationship to `Config.getDefault` needs to be explained, rather than merely adding a pathname.

These gaps do not change the scope of the current decision. What has been established is the public contract of the default configuration object; what remains to be added is the node semantics and any potential direct relationship they may have with the capture strategy.

Another earlier idea was to classify things in the opposite direction: since capture policy could affect capture scope, relegate both version and capture policy to supplementary information for node snapshots. This idea was not adopted either. When version and capture policy entered the discussion, they concerned the scope of checks on the configuration object; relegating them to snapshot side notes would once again let node names swallow up the object contract.

## Two Additional Notes from the Review

The subsequent review did not provide a complete node design, nor did it provide all the configuration keys. What it left were two more specific requirements for reading the material.

The first concerns "default configuration." Seeing just one key does not justify declaring the object complete; finding just one object entry point does not justify declaring that the extension reads all possible keys. The review required "the object as a whole" and "individual fields" to be documented separately. This requirement later became a prerequisite for checking version and capture policy: they are categories of keys that need to be verified, not a complete field list invented by the documentation.

The second concerns how nodes are described. shadow DOM descendants and slot assignment snapshots should not be used as synonyms. The former emphasizes descendant objects in the shadow tree; the latter emphasizes the snapshot context formed by slot assignment. They can be closely related within a capture discussion, but they cannot be used interchangeably just because both concern nodes. Ordinary ordered child nodes should also retain their own object name, because ordering itself is a distinct point of discussion.

These two marginal notes were brief, but their substance changed how the page was written. Any future addition of shadow-tree material must first make clear whether it is discussing descendants, ordered child nodes, or slot assignment. Any future addition of configuration material must first make clear whether it is discussing the object as a whole or a particular known key. If these distinctions are skipped, the old classification will reappear in different wording.

## Old Example 1: Import Names Mistaken for Responsibility Names

Someone once inferred from `MxWcStorage` at the top of the configuration file that the default configuration must be tied to the save process, and then inferred from `T` that it included shadow-tree handling. This example did not become a formal conclusion, but it is worth retaining on the page as an earlier reading error.

Import relationships only establish local adjacency for the current file. Names appearing related does not mean responsibilities have been explained. In this history in particular, configuration objects and node objects were already easy to conflate because they shared a page; inferring responsibilities from import names on top of that would disguise the missing material as a seemingly natural implementation diagram.

This old example now serves only as a reminder of the reading order: first distinguish whether you are investigating the object contract or node semantics, then decide whether file adjacency can help locate the relevant material. It cannot support any further assertions about storage, tools, or shadow-tree implementation.

## Old Example 2: Abbreviating Slot Snapshots as Descendants

An earlier text once suggested that, for brevity, slot assignment snapshots could be used directly in place of shadow DOM descendants. That abbreviation was not retained.

The slot-assignment snapshot and the shadow-tree descendants are distinct object terms. Even if a single capture process needs to observe both, the distinction cannot be removed with the expectation that the caller will restore it on its own. If the material addresses only slot assignment, it can only fill in the slot snapshot; if it addresses only ordered child nodes, it can only fill in the ordering; if it is meant to explain shadow-tree descendants, it must directly use "shadow-tree descendants" as the scope.

The old example is retained nearby because it reveals another risk on the shared page: compressing multiple objects into one label to make a sentence concise. The misreading of "local defaults" in the configuration section and the misreading of "snapshot nodes" in the node section actually have the same root cause: both turn objects that have not yet been fully checked into names convenient for categorization.

## State adopted by the current page

For ease of maintenance, this page depicts only the flow of historical judgments as states; it does not depict them as a runtime structure. The states in the diagram indicate how a particular judgment in the document is retained, reviewed, or discarded; they do not indicate that default configuration flows into the shadow tree, nor that configuration files are responsible for node snapshots.

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Shared record
    Shared record --> File entry retained
    Shared record --> Configuration object pending review
    Shared record --> Node object pending review
    File entry retained --> Entry not treated as a boundary
    Configuration object pending review --> Old local-defaults claim discarded
    Node object pending review --> Slot snapshot not used as an alias
    Entry not treated as a boundary --> Current layering
    Old local-defaults claim discarded --> Current layering
    Slot snapshot not used as an alias --> Current layering
```

The most important step in the diagram is "Entry not treated as a boundary." It preserves why the old investigation began with `src/js/lib/config.js`, and it removes the interpretation that automatically expands the path to include all technical ownership. The configuration object and node object continue to exist separately; an entry is no longer required to stand in for the other object when reaching a conclusion.

## Cross-cutting issue still not separated out

There is still a neighboring issue on the page: when the capture strategy changes, whether subsequent checks need to inspect the shadow tree, slot assignment, and ordinary ordered child nodes simultaneously. This issue has not been removed because it can indeed affect both the configuration side and the node side.

But for now it is only a cross-cutting issue, not an established causal relationship. One cannot infer from "the strategy may affect the scope of checks" that "the strategy defines all node rules"; nor can one infer from "node rules still need to be supplemented" that "version and capture strategy do not belong within the scope of default configuration." The former error would expand configuration keys into node design, while the latter would reduce the content of objects already requiring confirmation to irrelevant details.

This issue is being left on this page for now, rather than moved into a separate node record, so that the original layering can still be found when more material on the relationships is added later. If direct material is available next time, first state clearly whether it changes the meaning of the configuration object, the scope of the node object, or adds an explicit relationship between the two. If all that is found is another path name, that should not be used to revive the old approach of settling the issue based on file location.

## 2025-07-29 Current Decision

Following the drafting notes, path rechecks, unfinished attempts at separation, retirement of the old classification, and review margin notes, the default configuration is no longer characterized as a "collection of local fallback values". The current decision concerns the publicly exposed object itself, not its file location or the node semantics of the shadow tree:

Config.getDefault exposes the complete baseline configuration object, including the version and capture policy keys used by the extension.

This decision replaces the earlier, narrower description with a requirement for the object as a whole. Here, complete refers to the baseline configuration object, not a field catalog invented on this page. version and capture policy are categories of keys used by the extension and must be confirmed along with the object contract; finding just one isolated value among them is not enough to mark the default configuration as fully verified.

Therefore, when discussing the default configuration, first take the baseline object returned by `Config.getDefault` as the unit of discussion, then confirm version and capture policy. The old file entry point can still be used to reconstruct the investigation history, and the imports at the top of the file can still serve as pointers for related reading, but neither can replace an assessment of this publicly exposed object. The current requirements for the configuration object are finalized here, while the old characterization that it "may just be a few fallback values" is retained only as a historical framing.

The current decision does not change the boundaries of the shadow-tree section. It does not include shadow DOM descendants in the definition of the default object, nor does it claim that shadow-tree descendants are directly determined by `Config.getDefault`. Discussions of the shadow tree must still distinguish descendants, ordinary ordered child nodes, and slot assignment snapshots; what this page has established is that these objects must not be collapsed into the same thing based on configuration file paths or configuration key names.

## Review Order After the Decision

When the default configuration needs to be confirmed, first examine the object contract exposed by `Config.getDefault`. To understand why the old records led to the configuration file, look back at `src/js/lib/config.js` and the visible imports. The first step confirms the current object, and the second reconstructs the historical navigation; do not reverse the order and once again infer the object's completeness from the path.

When addressing the shadow-tree topic, first confirm whether the question concerns shadow DOM descendants, ordered child nodes, or slot assignment snapshots. Only after the object in question has been confirmed can we decide which layer the follow-up material should be added to. We must not replace all these references with "node snapshots" just because all these terms appear within the capture scope.

The shared page will continue to be retained, but the reason is different from that in the year 2023: it is no longer because the two topics have no boundaries between them, but because their shared records, misreadings, corrections, and current layering remain visible here as a continuous record. If they are split in the future, the old proposals, review margin notes, and this configuration object decision should be migrated according to their relationships, rather than moving only the final requirement sentence.

## For the Next Review

The following questions have not been resolved by this page:

- A direct description of shadow DOM descendants in specific snapshots still needs to be added separately;
- The relationship between slot assignment snapshots and shadow-tree descendants cannot be inferred from the similarity of their names;
- How ordinary ordered child nodes are handled cannot be inferred from the completeness of the default configuration object;
- If a new default configuration entry point appears, its relationship to `Config.getDefault` needs to be explained, rather than merely adding a path name.

These gaps do not change the scope of the current decision. What has now been established is the public contract for the default configuration object; what still needs to be added is node semantics and any direct relationship they may have with the capture strategy.

# Request Parameters and Slot Snapshot Plan

This proposal started from a single file, and only later did we realize that "adjacent" has two meanings: name-based adjacency and joint consumption of the same runtime object. `src/js/lib/request-params.js` remains an entry point in the former sense. Earlier records placed request, browser, and slot assignment snapshots in the same investigation section, so early designs tended to combine them; that path lacks sufficient local evidence and remains an option that was considered, not the default design.

One review narrowed the issue to the observable shape of request context. The factory result can be compared independently, while slot assignment snapshots should enter the same interface only after the actual save point and read point can both be matched. Do not add implicit conversion between them or infer call order from field names. If later we find only an export that generates request parameters but cannot find a direct read location for the snapshots, the record stops here; that does not mean filling the gap with a new module.

The current interface example is now finalized as:

RequestParams.createExample returns a request context that preserves the caller's refUrl while supplying stable frame and browser defaults.

This sentence constrains only the observable behavior of request context. It does not turn `slot assignment snapshots` into a return field on the factory, nor does it say whether the snapshot should be taken before or after frame creation. The experiment in the proposal is therefore split into two parts: first, use the same `refUrl` to compare context results under default and explicitly supplied browser settings; then, once the actual snapshot save point can be found, compare slot assignment before and after saving. If there is no entry point for the second part, do not simulate the caller or manually assemble a result that "looks the same."

The options and trade-offs are now:

- Conservative option: Keep the factory interface narrow, and let the existing save point continue managing snapshots. This has the lowest migration cost, at the cost of callers still needing to know when to save.
- Adapter option: Add a very thin adapter outside the factory that passes only the confirmed context to the snapshot save point. It can isolate the migration, but it cannot be used to slip in unconfirmed slot fields.
- Merge option: Extend the factory's return object to carry both context and the snapshot. Re-evaluate this only if, in the same revision, it is confirmed that both are created by the same stage and existing call sites do not depend on extra fields; not selected at present.

Acceptance materials retain only the correspondence between the diff and the actual results. For request context, check whether `refUrl` is retained by the caller and whether the frame and browser defaults are stable; for snapshots, check whether the save point and read point refer to the same object. If the results prove only the former, do not mark the latter as passed. If the parameter positions in an existing call change, a default value changes, or the snapshot is rewritten by a second stage, immediately roll back the adapter, restore the original factory shape, and leave the unconfirmed read point for the next focused check.

The responsibility boundary narrows accordingly: this page only decides the experimental direction for the request parameter factory; it does not decide implementation ownership on behalf of the maintainers of slot assignment snapshots. The entry point for further inspection remains `src/js/lib/request-params.js` and its direct neighbors in the current revision; do not merge the related objects into a shared contract before they are confirmed.

# Resource Type and Plan Conversion Troubleshooting Tree

Start by checking type before the resource task is enqueued. Incident reports often roll two symptoms into one: a resource task already exists but has the wrong media kind, or no assistant plan state is left to inspect after classification. Don't lump these together as "the image wasn't processed."

The old entry point was `src/js/capturer/picture.js`. When an issue is reported, first record the pre-call URL and MIME, and whether a resource task has already been created. If both URL and MIME are missing, stop at the inputs; don't guess the media kind from null values or go straight to the assistant plan.

When both URL and MIME are available, the old approach was to narrow the search using the URL suffix first. This approach is only suitable for quickly finding old records: if the suffix and MIME point in different directions, keep both; don't manually change them to match. If no resource task exists yet, go back to the pre-call inputs. If the task exists but kind doesn't match, keep the investigation focused on classification.

```text
Resource did not proceed as expected
├─ URL and MIME both missing
│  └─ Stop: provide the missing pre-call inputs
├─ Only one of URL or MIME was retained
│  └─ Keep the available input and task state
├─ Resource task not created
│  └─ Stop before task creation
├─ Task exists but kind doesn't match
│  └─ Keep URL, MIME, and the value on the task
└─ kind recorded but plan missing
   └─ Check for a plan before and after conversion separately
```

For assistant plan records, first check whether a plan existed before conversion. If there was no plan before conversion, don't label it a conversion failure. Only stop at conversion if a plan existed beforehand but the object can't be found afterward. If the object can still be found after conversion but nothing happens next, record that as a separate symptom; don't go back and revise the classification result.

When an old ticket has only URL left, you can use the suffix to find the general location, but that location doesn't mean MIME has been confirmed. The same applies if only MIME is left: it can preserve an input clue, but it can't replace the task state. If no resource task was created, an empty plan downstream doesn't help locate the issue.

Whether an empty resource enters the same branch is still unconfirmed. Keep that question open; it may stop before task creation, or the symptom may only appear later as a missing plan.

# Resource Type and Plan Conversion Troubleshooting Tree

This page still starts before the resource task enters the queue, but the earlier approach of putting incorrect kind and a missing assistant plan on the same track is no longer sufficient. The two things can happen consecutively, or only one of them may occur. At a minimum, records must distinguish the inputs before the call, the resource task, and the plans before and after conversion; record subsequent events separately, and do not use them to replace the state at any earlier point.

The old entry point is still `src/js/capturer/picture.js`. The only adjacencies directly visible in the file header are:

```js
import T from '../lib/tool.js';
import CaptureTool from './tool.js';
import SnapshotNodeChange from '../snapshot/change.js';
```

These items only identify positions on the picture capture side that can be reviewed further; they do not mean that any single object is solely responsible for resource classification or event publishing. Earlier records treated `CaptureTool` as the sole source of kind; there is currently insufficient evidence to support that attribution. The old wording remains here because some old incident tickets contain only this name, and removing it would make it impossible to see why people went straight there at the time.

## First separate the inputs from the task

When taking over a reproduction, first write down whether URL exists, whether MIME exists, and whether the resource task has already been created. A summary such as "image failed" or "plan missing" alone cannot later distinguish missing input, a classification anomaly, or an interruption during conversion.

```text
Obtain resource record
├─ URL missing
│  ├─ MIME also missing
│  │  └─ Stop: supply the input; do not write a kind conclusion
│  └─ MIME exists
│     └─ Retain MIME, task status, and the kind observed
├─ URL exists, MIME missing
│  └─ Retain URL, task status, and the kind observed
└─ URL and MIME both exist
   ├─ Point toward similar media categories
   │  └─ Check whether the resource task has appeared
   └─ Point toward different categories
      └─ Retain both side by side, then check the classification call
```

The stopping points in this tree must not be omitted. When the inputs are incomplete, do not infer a category from an empty value; when the resource task has not appeared, do not classify the absence of a later assistant plan as a conversion failure. First fill in enough to determine that part, then continue. If the task has been created but kind was not recorded, record only this gap; do not infer kind from whether the page shows any action.

Earlier on-call staff would use URL having an extension as the first entry point. This habit is not entirely useless: old records with only URL can still use it first to narrow the scope of the lookup. The problem is that it did not require retaining MIME, much less state whether the task had already appeared. Therefore, it can explain the shape of old records, but cannot replace the input pair and task status in new records.

## When URL and MIME are inconsistent

When URL and MIME both exist but point toward different media categories, do not first choose one and rewrite it as the "correct value." Retain the original URL, the original MIME, whether the resource task was created, and the classification value actually visible on the task side side by side. This lets later review distinguish three things: the inputs themselves are inconsistent, the task has a value close to one of them, or the task has not been generated at all.

Even if URL and MIME look similar, do not delete the other one. Similarity only means there is no obvious conflict at present; it does not mean classification is complete, much less that a plan has been generated. Old tickets often leave only one suffix and a sentence saying "looks like an image"; with such material, record only the items that can still be seen in the supplemental notes, and do not fabricate MIME or the kind on the task.

```text
Inputs retained so far
├─ URL and MIME both exist
│  ├─ Directions are similar
│  │  └─ Continue confirming whether the task was created
│  └─ Directions are different
│     └─ Preserve the conflict, then trace back through the classification call
├─ Only URL remains
│  └─ Do not record the suffix as a MIME conclusion
├─ Only MIME remains
│  └─ Do not record MIME as a URL conclusion
└─ Neither exists
   └─ Stop at the inputs; do not enter the plan branch
```

## The kind on the task is not the conclusion for the whole chain

During review, write task status and kind separately. If the task does not exist, stop before task creation; if the task exists but no visible kind is present, the issue remains around classification; if the task has a kind that does not match the inputs, retain the inputs and that value; if the task has a kind that appears usable, that only means a classification result was visible on the task at that time.

Previously there was a shortcut: as long as the kind on the task pointed in the same direction as the suffix of URL, jump directly to the assistant plan. This is now retained as a legacy path. It skipped MIME, and did not record whether the classification value came from URL, MIME, or another call site. When an anomaly in which URL conflicts with MIME is encountered, it discards the information most worth reviewing.

```text
Resource task
├─ Not created
│  └─ Return to the pre-call inputs; stop this section
├─ Created, no kind
│  └─ Retain task status; return to the classification location
├─ Created, kind does not match the input
│  └─ Retain URL, MIME, and kind; do not manually change them
└─ Created, visible kind present
   └─ The assistant plan before conversion can be checked
```

Here, "can be checked" does not require following every record further. Some anomalies are sufficiently addressed by proving that the task has not yet been created or that the inputs already conflict, so it is enough to stop in the earlier section. Do not record an unobserved plan status as absent just because you want to make a record complete.

## The plan must be examined starting before conversion

For plan-related records, retain at least two points: whether an assistant plan exists before conversion, and whether the corresponding object can still be found after conversion. If it is empty before conversion, first return to the resource task; only when it exists before conversion but there is no object after conversion should you stop at conversion. If both ends are present but no subsequent action is visible on the page, list it separately under publishing; do not delete the converted object and then guess.

```text
Assistant plan did not continue
├─ No plan before conversion
│  ├─ Resource task does not exist
│  │  └─ Return to the pre-call inputs; stop
│  └─ Resource task exists
│     └─ Retain kind and inputs; do not call it a conversion failure
├─ Present before conversion, no object after conversion
│  └─ Stop at conversion; retain the before-and-after objects
└─ Object still present after conversion
   ├─ Subsequent events visible
   │  └─ End this page here
   └─ Subsequent events not visible
      └─ Record the publishing-side symptom separately
```

In the past, writing "did not see an event" directly under conversion anomalies collapsed two situations into one phrase: one where there was no plan before conversion, and another where the object remained after conversion but subsequent events were simply not observed. These two cases require different lookup locations and cannot both be assigned to the same section of picture capture.

## Notes retained

There is still no single position for an empty resource that can support a definitive conclusion. It may stop before task creation, or it may only manifest as no plan at a later stage; this page does not contain enough material to choose between the two possibilities. Do not substitute missing URL, missing MIME, and an empty resource for one another.

When you need to continue checking where the classification value came from, start from these three visible adjacencies—`T`, `CaptureTool`, and `SnapshotNodeChange`—and review the actual call records. When you need to continue checking events, start a separate publishing-side record. Retain the old suffix-first section solely to explain why early troubleshooting was left with only URL; do not use it as a way to adjudicate conflicting inputs.

Stop recording once a given section is already missing an input or object. Compared with combining classification, conversion, and events into one failure name, leaving a clear stopping point makes it easier for later review to pick up.

Such wording made handoffs easier at the time, but it lumped classification, resource tasks, plan conversion, and subsequent events together. The tree, marginal notes, and old shorthand added later were not cleaned out; they describe troubleshooting entry points at different times, and also explain why some historical entries contain only URL, a kind, or the phrase "the plan was not produced".

The current entry point for reviewing this is still `src/js/capturer/picture.js`. The connections directly visible at the top of the file are as follows:

```js
import CaptureTool from './tool.js';
import SnapshotNodeChange from '../snapshot/change.js';
```

The earliest rules started with the URL suffix. At the time, the incidents involved only page input and a few task records, and the approach was to first look for a URL that looked like an image, then check for a corresponding task; if the task had a kind, the next step was to look for the assistant plan. This approach was documented only roughly, but it is still useful when reviewing old entries from the same period.

```text
Old shorthand
Resource did not proceed
├─ URL looks like an image
│  └─ Look for task
│     ├─ Has kind: check assistant plan
│     └─ No kind: stay at classification
└─ URL is unclear
   └─ Then check MIME
```

The old tree did not require first confirming whether a resource task had actually been created, nor did it require recording URL and MIME together. It documents how the search was narrowed down at the time, not rules for resolving conflicting inputs. "Has kind" in the old entries also only meant that a value was seen on the task at the time; this cannot be taken to mean that the basis for classification was complete, much less that plan conversion or subsequent events had already completed.

During the same period, "no plan appeared" was also used as a catch-all label for the conversion stage. This label did not distinguish between there being no plan at all before conversion, no object being found after conversion, and the object still being present but subsequent events not being observed. Historical searches may still turn up this phrase, so the original wording is retained; it is no longer sufficient as a stopping point for current investigations.

There was an unresolved side note at the time: whether an empty resource was the same as a missing URL. The old records did not provide an answer. Some records retained only empty inputs, while others did not show the absence of a plan until later. Lumping all of them under an empty URL would erase the distinction between whether a resource task had already been generated or not.

## 2023-03: Stopping points in the on-call margins

After the old tree was reviewed, two very small checks were added in the margin: first check whether the pre-call inputs were retained, and first check whether a resource task had appeared. The old tree was not rewritten, only stopping conditions were added to subsequent records. The point was not to claim that anomalies did not exist, but to avoid arbitrarily assigning an anomaly to classification, conversion, or publishing when the available evidence was insufficient.

```text
Pre-call inputs
├─ URL, MIME are both missing
│  └─ Stop: add the missing inputs, do not record a media type
├─ Only URL remains
│  └─ Retain URL and the task status
├─ Only MIME remains
│  └─ Retain MIME and the task status
└─ Both are present
   └─ Retain both, then check the task
```

When both inputs are missing, the category cannot be filled in based on the behavior on the page. When a resource task has not been created, a conversion failure must not be recorded outright just because no assistant plan appears afterward. Previously, investigations would go all the way from empty inputs to picture capture, ultimately leaving an unsupported guess about the media; this side note requires stopping at the inputs.

A record with only URL remaining also does not mean that URL is already sufficient. It can help someone find an old call by its suffix, but it cannot replace MIME. The same applies when only MIME remains: it can show that an input field existed at the time, but it cannot replace URL, the task status, or the classification result. Old incident tickets often contained only one of the two items, and supplemental notes can only restore material that is still visible, not manufacture the other input for historical records.

## Scope of the old rules

The early approach was "if URL has an extension, use the suffix first; if URL has no information, then check MIME". This sequence quickly narrowed the scope at the time, so it was not removed. It helps explain why older on-call records often contain only URL, and can also help you start reviewing near the old entry point.

However, it is not a rule for choosing between URL and MIME when they conflict. When both inputs are present but point in different directions, retaining only the suffix leaves later reviewers unable to tell which input the task's kind came from. If either input is manually rewritten to match the other, subsequent classification reviews lose the original clues.

The old rule is also no substitute for checking task creation. Just because URL looks like an image does not mean that a resource task already exists; having a kind on the task also does not mean that this kind is sufficient to explain how the input was classified. Linking "looks like an image" directly to "check the plan" is a limitation of the early shorthand, not the sequence new records should follow.

## 2023-07: Breaking down the situation in a single review

Later reviews no longer started by asking whether anything happened on the page, but instead broke each record down into five points: the inputs before the call, the resource task, the assistant plan before conversion, the object after conversion, and subsequent events. This is the order in which information is recorded, not proof of causality. Its purpose is to prevent later-stage symptoms from obscuring earlier-stage objects that have already been confirmed.

| Point | What should have been recorded at the time | What cannot be inferred directly from this |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before the call | Whether URL and MIME exist | Classification definitely succeeded |
| Resource task | Whether it has been created and whether it has a kind | A plan was definitely generated |
| Before conversion | Whether there is an assistant plan | Subsequent events have already occurred |
| After conversion | Whether the object can still be found | The caller definitely received it |
| Events | Whether they were found | The preceding conversion must be faulty |

Each row in the table can be a stopping point. If inputs are missing, stop at the inputs; if the task has not been created, stop before creation; if there is no plan before conversion, preserve that state rather than relabeling it as a conversion failure; if the object is still present after conversion but no event is found, leave that observation for the publishing side. Not every anomaly requires all five rows to be filled in.

Compared with the old tree, the branches used during review added two areas covering task creation and before/after the plan:

```text
Resource did not continue as expected
├─ Neither URL nor MIME was retained before the call
│  └─ Stop at input; backfill the collection records
├─ The resource task was not created
│  └─ Stop before task creation
├─ The task was created, but kind does not match
│  └─ Retain URL, MIME, and the classification value on the task
└─ The task already has a visible kind
   ├─ No assistant plan before conversion
   │  └─ Return to the task; do not record it as a conversion failure
   ├─ An object existed before conversion, but none existed after conversion
   │  └─ Stop at conversion
   └─ An object still exists after conversion
      └─ Investigate subsequent events separately
```

Here, "visible kind" is only a logging term. It means that the task had a classification value visible at the time; it does not mean that URL and MIME are already consistent, nor that the source of the category has been confirmed. An old ticket with only URL and kind can still use this tree to find the stopping point; the missing MIME cannot be backfilled in an addendum with an inferred value.

## Failed Reverse-Inference Approach

During review, we abandoned an approach that inferred the entire chain backward from page results: whenever the page had no subsequent action, it treated the plan as missing both before and after, and listed the classification as pending investigation as well. This approach appeared to reduce a few lookbacks, but in practice it could not distinguish between there having been no plan at all before conversion and the object still being present after conversion with only the event missing.

Once these two scenarios were covered by the same "plan lost" label, resource classification was also pulled in for no reason. The first should return to the task and input; the second should retain the object after conversion, then move to the publishing side. If both are recorded as conversion failures, later investigators will look in the wrong section for an object that was not there in the first place.

At the time, we also treated the task's kind and the suffix of URL pointing in similar directions as evidence that "classification was complete." This judgment was likewise insufficient: it did not retain MIME, nor explain which call site supplied the value on the resource task. In old tickets with no conflicting input, it could help locate the relevant point, but it could not replace a recheck of the classification.

Therefore, the following old handling is marked as no longer applicable: first guess the category from the suffix of URL; if a kind pointing in a similar direction is seen in the task, inspect the plan directly; if no plan is found, mark it as pending conversion investigation. The three steps respectively drop MIME, treat a single value on the task as complete evidence, and skip the pre-conversion state and the event side. The old handling remains in the document to explain why historical records contain only these fields.

## Addendum for Input Conflicts

Later, records frequently appeared with both URL and MIME present, but pointing toward different media types. The earlier suffix-first approach could only narrow the scope, not provide a final determination. For these records, first retain the original URL, the original MIME, whether a resource task was created, and the classification value actually visible on the task, side by side.

Do not modify URL, do not replace MIME, and do not manually rewrite kind to make the record look consistent. If the inputs conflict and the task has not yet been created, stop before task creation; if the task has been created but kind does not match one of the inputs, simply preserve this set of relationships and continue tracing the actual calls to find where classification takes place. The conflict itself is part of the state to preserve, not a formatting issue to smooth over.

```text
Input retained so far
├─ URL, MIME both present
│  ├─ Point in similar directions
│  │  └─ Continue checking whether the task was created
│  └─ Point in different directions
│     └─ Preserve the conflict and trace back through the classification calls
├─ Only URL remains
│  └─ Do not record the suffix as a MIME conclusion
├─ Only MIME remains
│  └─ Do not record MIME as a URL conclusion
└─ Neither is present
   └─ Stop at the input, do not enter the plan branch
```

Inputs pointing in similar directions are still no reason to omit either one. This only means there is no obvious conflict at present, not that classification is complete, much less that a plan has been generated. For older entries that retain only URL and the phrase "looks like an image", you can still use URL to find the old entry point, but you must not backfill MIME, task status, or conversion results.

On the resource task side, these states also need to be recorded separately: not created, created but without kind, created with a kind mismatch, and created with a visible kind. Only the last case provides grounds to continue checking the assistant plan before conversion; the first three do not automatically count as plan anomalies just because no subsequent action appears on the page.

```text
Resource task
├─ Not created
│  └─ Return to the pre-call input; stop this section
├─ Created, no kind
│  └─ Preserve the task state, return to the classification point
├─ Created, kind does not match the input
│  └─ Preserve URL, MIME, kind, do not edit manually
└─ Created, kind is visible
   └─ You can inspect the assistant plan before conversion
```

## Branches in the conversion stage

Troubleshooting the assistant plan must start before conversion. When there is no plan before conversion, the issue cannot yet be described as a conversion failure; first verify the resource task and the pre-call input. Only when there is a plan before conversion but no object afterward should you stop at the conversion point. When the object still exists after conversion, the presence or absence of events should be recorded as a separate observation.

```text
assistant plan did not continue as expected
├─ No plan before conversion
│  ├─ Resource task does not exist
│  │  └─ Return to the pre-call input; stop
│  └─ Resource task exists
│     └─ Record kind and the input; do not classify this as a conversion failure
├─ Plan exists before conversion, no object after conversion
│  └─ Stop at the conversion point, preserve the before-and-after objects
└─ Object still exists after conversion
   ├─ Subsequent events found
   │  └─ This page ends here
   └─ Subsequent events not found
      └─ Record this separately on the publishing side, do not retroactively reclassify it as a missing plan
```

The focus of this tree is its stopping conditions. When the resource task does not exist, you cannot skip over the task state and discuss conversion; when the object exists after conversion, you also cannot conclude that conversion did not occur just because the caller has not observed an event yet. A single anomaly can involve states from multiple stages at the same entry point, and sharing an entry point does not mean they can be combined into a single conclusion.

When there is no plan before conversion, preserve the actual state of the resource task and the input. At this point even if the task has a kind, that only indicates that the task record reached that point; it does not by itself prove that a plan should have appeared. When there is a plan before conversion but no object afterward, the before-and-after objects are the most important material to retain for the conversion stage. When the object still exists after conversion, this page should not go on to explain on behalf of the publishing side whether the event was received.

## Boundaries when reviewing files

`src/js/capturer/picture.js` is the entry point referenced by older anomaly records. The references `T`,`CaptureTool`,`SnapshotNodeChange` in the file header can serve as adjacent points for continuing to inspect the actual calls, but they cannot be used as grounds for identifying any one item as the sole owner. In particular regarding the earlier claim that directly identified `CaptureTool` as the sole source of kind, there are no longer enough records to support it.

When continuing the investigation from this entry point, start with the URL, MIME, task state and before-and-after plan states already available in the current context. If there is no corresponding call record, stop at the current observations, and do not turn import names into causal attributions. The classification and conversion stages require different objects; subsequent events are recorded separately, so a single file path should not be used to explain everything.

If an old ticket only has URL, you can start looking on the picture capture side; if it only has MIME, you should also retain MIME itself before checking the task state; if neither is present, do not proceed to determining the kind. If an old ticket only says "plan is missing", first identify whether this means no plan before conversion, no object after conversion, or no event found; if no match can be made, retain the old wording, without forcing it into a stage.

## Disagreements remaining after reviewing the records

When reviewing old records, one tendency is to stop retaining URL and MIME whenever the task has a visible kind. This makes the records a little shorter, but if the inputs conflict, people reviewing them later cannot tell where the value on the task came from. Another tendency is to require the entire chain to be traced in one pass whenever an assistant plan ultimately has no follow-up action. This appears to reduce handoffs, but each time it requires obtaining event-side material that may not exist.

The retained approach falls between the two: retain the input pair and the classification value on the task for the classification stage; retain the before-and-after plan states for the conversion stage; only record whether an event appeared for the event stage. If any stage lacks an object or input, you can stop at that stage, without substituting the previous stage's normal or abnormal status for it.

This material still does not assign empty resources to a fixed branch. They should not automatically be treated as conversion anomalies because there is no plan, nor should they automatically be considered the same kind of resource because the inputs are empty. To continue deciding where to handle them, a record is needed that captures the inputs before the call, the task state and the before-and-after plan states together; there is currently no such record to support grouping them together.

## The current classification point

Task.getResourceType classifies a URL or MIME pair into a stable media kind before a resource task is queued.

This requirement defines the inputs to classification and where it occurs. When handling anomalies, first confirm whether the classification point before resource task queuing has been reached; if the task has already been queued but its kind is abnormal, return to the classification stage to continue; if it has not been queued, first return to the inputs or task creation. It does not mean that an assistant plan necessarily exists, nor does it mean that subsequent events have necessarily already been published.

New records can capture the context in the short format below. Square brackets only indicate where to record information, and do not require inventing values that have not been observed:

```text
Input: URL [present/absent]; MIME [present/absent]
Task: [not created/created]; kind [value observed/not recorded]
Plan: before conversion [present/absent]; after conversion [present/absent]
Event: [found/not found/not checked]
Stopped at: [input/task/conversion/event]
```

If only URL or only MIME is known, write only the item that actually exists. If the resource task has not been created, the record can stop at the task line; if the post-conversion object is still present, the event line can be recorded separately. Do not try to complete the format by filling in gaps, using inferred values for missing inputs, plan or events.

## Related issues and legacy appendix

If the post-conversion object exists but no event is found, continue investigating on the publishing side. DOC-14 are related entry points; the approach retained on this page avoids feeding publishing-side symptoms back into conclusions about classification or plan conversion. The specific paths for handling empty resources and assistant event publication are not documented here.

Below is the shorthand left over from 2023, still retained for people reviewing old tickets, but no longer suitable as a basis for current operational conclusions:

```text
If a resource does not progress:
1. Check whether URL looks like an image;
2. If it does, check task;
3. If task exists but there is still no result, check assistant plan;
4. If there is no plan, record it as conversion.
```

The problems are in step 1 and step 4: the former does not retain MIME, so conflicting inputs get suppressed; the latter does not distinguish between no plan before conversion, no object after conversion and an event that has not appeared. The old shorthand can still explain why historical records contain only URL or the word "conversion", but it cannot cover the new stage records.
