# Current contract notice

Revision: capture-pipeline-r3-20260920. The field, token and migration inventory is DOC-49; older notes below are historical context, not a restriction on the cumulative assignment. Feature decisions are reachable from the named owners. Pending means unresolved, not nonexistent.

# Resource Type and Plan Conversion Troubleshooting Tree

These notes originally supported incident tickets for picture capture. Descriptions in old tickets were often very brief: the task's media type was wrong, or the assistant plan did not proceed. That wording made handoffs easier at the time, but it lumped classification, resource tasks, plan conversion, and subsequent events together. The tree, margin notes, and old shorthand added later were not cleaned up; they describe troubleshooting entry points from different times, and also explain why some historical entries contain only URL, a kind, or the phrase "the plan did not appear".

The current starting point for review is still `src/js/capturer/picture.js`. The directly visible connections at the top of the file are as follows:

```js
import T from '../lib/tool.js';
import CaptureTool from './tool.js';
import SnapshotNodeChange from '../snapshot/change.js';
```

These imports are useful for continuing to trace actual calls from the picture capture side. They do not establish ownership: seeing `CaptureTool` does not mean resource classification takes place only in that object; seeing `SnapshotNodeChange` does not mean it is responsible for assistant plan conversion or event publishing. When handling an incident, first retain the inputs and objects already observed, then decide which stage to stop at, rather than drawing premature conclusions from filenames.

## 2023-03: The Initial Shorthand

The earliest rules started with the URL suffix. At the time, the incidents being investigated had only page input and a few task records available, so the approach was to first find a URL that looked like an image, then check whether there was a corresponding task; when the task had a kind, the search continued for an assistant plan. This approach was recorded only roughly, but it is still useful when reviewing old entries from the same period.

```text
Old shorthand notes
The resource did not proceed
├─ URL looks like an image
│  └─ Find the task
│     ├─ Has kind: check assistant plan
│     └─ No kind: stay at classification
└─ URL is unclear
   └─ Check MIME again
```

The old tree did not require first confirming whether the resource task had actually been created, nor did it require recording URL and MIME together. It documented how the search scope was narrowed at the time, not the rules for resolving conflicting inputs. The "has kind" in the old entry also only meant that a value was seen on the task at the time; this does not establish that the basis for classification was complete, much less that plan conversion or subsequent events had already completed.

During the same period "the plan did not appear" was also used as a blanket term for the conversion stage. This blanket term did not distinguish between there being no plan at all before conversion, no object being found after conversion, and the object still being present but no subsequent events being observed. Searches of historical records may still match this phrase, so the original wording is retained; it is no longer sufficient to serve as the current stopping point.

There was an unresolved side note at the time: whether an empty resource was the same as a missing URL. The old records provided no answer. Some records retained only empty input, while others did not show that there was no plan until a later point. If all of them are lumped together as cases where URL is empty, the distinction of whether the resource task had already been generated would disappear.

## 2023-03: Stopping points in the on-call margins

After the old tree was reviewed, two very small checks were added in the margins: check first whether the pre-call input was retained, and check first whether the resource task appeared. The old tree was not rewritten, only stopping conditions were added to subsequent records. The point was not to claim that no anomaly existed, but to avoid arbitrarily assigning an anomaly to classification, conversion or publishing when there was not enough information.

```text
Pre-call input
├─ Neither URL nor MIME is present
│  └─ Stop: add the missing input, do not record a media type
├─ Only URL remains
│  └─ Retain URL and the task status
├─ Only MIME remains
│  └─ Retain MIME and the task status
└─ Both items are present
   └─ Retain both items, then check the task
```

When both inputs are missing, do not infer the category from the behavior on the page. When no resource task has been created, do not mark the conversion as failed just because no assistant plan appears afterward. Previously, investigations would trace empty inputs all the way to picture capture, ultimately leaving behind an unsupported guess about the media; this side note requires stopping at the inputs.

A record with only URL remaining does not mean that URL is sufficient, either. It can help someone locate an old call by its suffix, but it cannot replace MIME. The same applies when only MIME remains: it can show that an input field was present at the time, but it cannot replace URL, the task status, or the classification result. Older incident tickets often contain only one of the two; supplemental notes can only add back material that is still visible, not fabricate the other input for historical records.

## Scope of the old rule

The early rule was "if URL has an extension, follow the suffix first; if URL provides no information, then look at MIME". This order could quickly narrow the scope at the time, so it was not removed. It can explain why old on-call records often contain only URL, and can also help start a review around the old entry point.

However, it is not a rule for choosing between URL and MIME when they conflict. When both inputs are present but point in different directions, keeping only the suffix leaves later readers unable to tell which input supplied the kind on the task. If either input is manually rewritten to match the other, subsequent classification reviews lose the original clues.

The old rule also cannot replace the task creation check. Just because URL looks like an image does not mean that a resource task already exists; having a kind on the task also does not mean that this kind is sufficient to explain how the input was classified. Going directly from "looks like an image" to "check the plan" is a limitation of the early shorthand, not the sequence that new records should follow.

## 2023-07: A review breaks down the case

Later reviews no longer started by asking whether there was any activity on the page, but instead broke a record down into five points: the inputs before the call, the resource task, the assistant plan before conversion, the object after conversion, and subsequent events. This is the order for recording information, not proof of causality. Its purpose is to prevent downstream symptoms from obscuring upstream objects that have already been confirmed.

| Location | What should have been retained at the time | What cannot be directly inferred from this |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before the call | Whether URL and MIME exist | Classification definitely succeeded |
| Resource task | Whether it has been created and whether it has a kind | plan was definitely generated |
| Before conversion | Whether there is an assistant plan | Subsequent events have already appeared |
| After conversion | Whether the object can still be found | The caller definitely received it |
| Event | Whether it was found | The preceding conversion must have been faulty |

Each row in the table can be a stopping point. When inputs are missing, stop at the inputs; when the task has not been created, stop before creation; when there is no plan before conversion, preserve that state rather than relabeling it as a conversion failure; when the object is still present after conversion but the event cannot be found, leave the issue on the publishing side. Not every anomaly requires all five rows to be filled in.

The branches used during review add two areas to the old tree: task creation and the stages before and after plan:

```text
Resource did not proceed as expected
├─ Before the call, neither URL nor MIME was retained
│  └─ Stop at the inputs; collect additional records
├─ Resource task was not created
│  └─ Stop before task creation
├─ Task was created but kind does not match
│  └─ Keep URL, MIME, and the classification value on the task
└─ Task already has a visible kind
   ├─ No assistant plan before conversion
   │  └─ Go back to the task; do not record this as a conversion failure
   ├─ Object present before conversion, absent after conversion
   │  └─ Stop at conversion
   └─ Object still present after conversion
      └─ Investigate subsequent events separately
```

Here, "visible kind" is just a term used in the records. It means the task has a classification value that was visible at the time; it does not mean that URL and MIME already match, nor does it mean that the source of the classification has been confirmed. When an old ticket contains only URL and kind, this tree can still be used to find the stopping point; the missing MIME must not be filled in with a guessed value in supplementary notes.

## A failed approach to reasoning backward

During review, an approach that inferred the entire chain backward from the page result was abandoned: whenever the page showed no follow-up action, it labeled plan as missing both before and after, and also listed classification as needing investigation. This approach seemed to save a few repeat checks, but in practice it could not distinguish between there being no plan at all before conversion and the object still being present after conversion with only the event failing to appear.

Once these two situations are covered by the same "plan loss" label, resource classification also gets dragged in without cause. The first should go back to the task and inputs; the second should retain the object after conversion, then move to the publishing side. If both are recorded as conversion failures, people following up will look in the wrong stage for an object that was never there in the first place.

At the time, the fact that kind on the task and the URL suffix pointed to similar media types was also treated as evidence of "classification complete". That judgment was also insufficient: it did not retain MIME, nor did it explain which call the value on the resource task came from. It could help with investigation in older tickets without conflicting inputs, but it could not replace tracing classification back to its source.

Therefore, the following old procedure is marked as no longer applicable: first guess the category from the URL suffix; if kind on the task points to a similar media type, go straight to the plan; if no plan can be found, mark it as pending conversion investigation. These three steps respectively suppressed MIME, treated a single task value as the complete basis for the judgment, and skipped the pre-conversion state and the event side. The old procedure remains in this document to explain why only these fields remain in the historical records.

## Addendum on conflicting inputs

Later, records began appearing in clusters in which URL and MIME were both present but pointed to different media types. The early suffix-first method could only narrow the scope, not provide a final determination. For such records, first retain the original URL, the original MIME, whether the resource task was created, and the classification value actually visible on the task, side by side.

Do not modify URL, do not replace MIME, and do not manually rewrite kind to make the record appear consistent. If the inputs conflict and the task has not yet been created, stop before task creation; if the task has been created but kind is inconsistent with one of the inputs, likewise retain only this set of relationships and continue following the actual calls to find where classification occurs. The conflict itself is evidence that must be preserved, not a formatting issue to smooth over.

```text
Inputs retained so far
├─ URL and MIME are both present
│  ├─ Point to similar media types
│  │  └─ Continue checking whether the task was created
│  └─ Point to different media types
│     └─ Preserve the conflict and trace back through the classification calls
├─ Only URL remains
│  └─ Do not record the suffix as a conclusion about MIME
├─ Only MIME remains
│  └─ Do not record MIME as a conclusion about URL
└─ Neither is present
   └─ Stop at the input, do not enter the plan branch
```

Similar input directions are not a reason to omit either item. This only means that there is no obvious conflict at present, not that classification is complete, much less that a plan has been generated. For old entries that retain only URL and the phrase "looks like an image", you can still use URL to find the old entry point, but must not backfill MIME, the task status, or the conversion result.

The resource task side also needs to record these cases separately: not created, created but without a kind, created with a mismatched kind, and created with a visible kind. Only the last case provides a reason to proceed with checking the assistant plan before conversion; the first three do not automatically become plan anomalies just because the page shows no subsequent actions.

```text
Resource task
├─ Not created
│  └─ Return to the pre-call input; stop this section
├─ Created, no kind
│  └─ Record the task status, return to the classification point
├─ Created, kind does not match the input
│  └─ Record URL, MIME, kind, do not edit manually
└─ Created, visible kind
   └─ The assistant plan before conversion can be checked
```

## Branches in the conversion stage

Troubleshooting the assistant plan must start before conversion. If there is no plan before conversion, the issue cannot yet be described as a conversion failure; first confirm the resource task and the pre-call input. Only when there is a plan before conversion but no object afterward should troubleshooting stop at conversion. If an object still exists after conversion, the presence or absence of events should be recorded as a separate observation.

```text
The assistant plan did not continue as expected
├─ No plan before conversion
│  ├─ Resource task does not exist
│  │  └─ Return to the pre-call input; stop
│  └─ Resource task exists
│     └─ Record kind and input; do not classify as a conversion failure
├─ Plan exists before conversion, no object after conversion
│  └─ Stop at conversion, retain the before-and-after objects
└─ Object still exists after conversion
   ├─ Subsequent events found
   │  └─ This page ends here
   └─ Subsequent events not found
      └─ Record separately on the publishing side, do not retroactively change this to a missing plan
```

The focus of this tree is its stopping conditions. When the resource task does not exist, you cannot skip the task status and move on to conversion; when the object exists after conversion, you also cannot reject the conversion just because the caller has not yet observed an event. A single incident can show multiple stages of status at the same entry point, and sharing an entry point does not mean they can be merged into one conclusion.

When there is no plan before conversion, retain the actual state of the resource task and input. Even if the task has a kind at this point, that only means the task has been recorded up to that point; it cannot by itself prove that a plan should have appeared. When there is a plan before conversion but no object afterward, the before-and-after objects are the most important materials to retain for the conversion stage. When the object still exists after conversion, this page should no longer explain on behalf of the publishing side whether the events were received.

`src/js/capturer/picture.js` is the entry point referenced by the old exception record. The file-header entries `T`,`CaptureTool`,`SnapshotNodeChange` can serve as nearby leads for further inspection of the actual calls, but they do not justify identifying any one item as the sole owner. In particular, the earlier claim that directly identified `CaptureTool` as the sole source of kind no longer has sufficient support in the records.

When continuing the investigation from this entry point, start with the URL, MIME, task status and before-and-after plan states already available in the incident context. If there is no corresponding call record, stop at the current observation, and do not turn an import name into an attribution. The classification and conversion stages require different objects; subsequent events belong to yet another part of the record, and a single file path should not be made to account for everything.

If an old ticket contains only URL, you can start looking on the picture capture side; if it contains only MIME, you should also retain MIME itself before checking the task status; if neither item is present, do not proceed to category determination. If an old ticket says only "plan is missing", first check which situation it corresponds to among no plan before conversion, no object after conversion, or event not found; if no match can be made, retain the old wording, and do not force it into a stage.

## Disagreements remaining after reviewing the records

When reviewing old records, one tendency is to stop retaining URL and MIME whenever the task has a visible kind. This makes the record a little shorter, but if the inputs conflict, those who come later cannot tell where the value on the task came from. Another tendency is to require tracing the entire chain in one pass whenever the assistant plan ultimately has no follow-up action. This appears to reduce handoffs, but requires obtaining event-side material every time even though it may not exist.

The retained approach lies between the two: retain the input pair and the classification value on the task in the classification stage; retain the before-and-after plan states in the conversion stage; record only whether the event appeared in the event stage. If any stage lacks an object or input, you can stop at that stage, without substituting the previous stage's normal or abnormal status for it.

This material still does not assign empty resources to any fixed branch. An empty resource should not automatically be counted as a conversion exception because it has no plan, nor should it automatically be treated as the same type of resource because the input is empty. To continue deciding where to handle it, a record is needed that captures the pre-call input, task status and before-and-after plan states together; there is currently no such record available as a basis for grouping them together.

## Current classification point

Task.getResourceType classifies a URL or MIME pair into a stable media kind before a resource task is queued.

This requirement defines the inputs to classification and where it occurs. When troubleshooting an issue, first confirm whether execution has reached the classification step before the resource task is queued; if the task has already been queued but its kind is unexpected, return to the classification section to continue; if it has not been queued, first return to the input or task creation. It does not mean that an assistant plan necessarily exists, nor does it mean that subsequent events have necessarily already been published.

New records can use the short format below to capture the observed state. The square brackets only indicate where to record information and do not require inventing values that have not been observed:

```text
Input: URL [present/absent]; MIME [present/absent]
Task: [not created/created]; kind [observed value/not recorded]
Plan: before conversion [present/absent]; after conversion [present/absent]
Event: [found/not found/not checked]
Stopped at: [input/task/conversion/event]
```

If only URL is known or only MIME is known, record only the item that actually exists. If the resource task has not been created, the record can stop at the task line; if the post-conversion object still exists, the event line can be recorded separately. Do not fill in missing inputs, plans, or events with guessed values just to complete the format.

If the post-conversion object exists but the event has not been found, move to the publication side to continue. DOC-14 are adjacent entry points; the approach retained on this page avoids working backward from publication-side symptoms to conclusions about classification or plan conversion. The specific paths for empty-resource handling and assistant event publication are not added here.

The following shorthand was recorded in 2023, is still retained for those reviewing old tickets, and is no longer suitable for drawing conclusions about current operations:

```text
If you see that a resource has not progressed:
1. Check whether URL looks like an image;
2. If it does, check task;
3. If task exists but there is still no result, check assistant plan;
4. If there is no plan, mark it as conversion.
```

The issue is in step 1 and step 4: the former did not retain MIME, so conflicting inputs are suppressed; the latter did not distinguish between no plan before conversion, no object after conversion, and the event not occurring. # Image Capture Policy Decision Record

This page originally aimed only to preserve one lookup habit: when an old issue involving image capture policy comes up, first look at `src/pages/background.js`. This habit came from issue names and call names, not from a complete implementation archive. The first draft put the two together, and the problem only became apparent later: readers knew which file to open, but could easily mistake that file's location for the place where the policy had been fully documented.

The file itself is still worth keeping in the record. When the old investigation reached this point, the direct dependencies visible at the top of the file were:

```js
import Log from '../js/lib/log.js';
import T from '../js/lib/tool.js';
import ExtApi from '../js/lib/ext-api.js';
import ExtMsg from '../js/lib/ext-msg.js';
```

These four lines were a local observation that could be consistently reproduced at the time. They show that background.js is not an isolated page with no connections: readers will at least encounter names related to logging, utilities, extension API, and messaging. They also explain why the old record did not start with an abstract "image rule," but instead paused at this js module. The top of the file did not contain an image selection table, much less set out the relationships among asset, source, attribute, browser, and resource. in an order that could be applied directly.

## The Decision in the First Draft

The choice in v1 was straightforward. The first option was to treat background.js as the entry point for the rules, without establishing another place to check afterward; the second was to retain only the path and the object relationships visible from it, then decide whether to expand the record when a review took place. The first draft favored the first option because the old investigation already had issue names and call names to trace, and looking for another entry point on the fly would only break the continuity of the record.

The decision at the time did not claim that all references had been read. It was more of a practical trade-off: first put image capture policy somewhere easy to find again, so the old issue would not leave behind only vague terms. The first draft also explicitly left two items blank: the current value of resource. and the priority relationship between attribute and source. However, the statement "background.js is the entry point for the rules" was too categorical and obscured the significance of those gaps.

The judgment in the old paragraph is still retained: tracing back from background.js can piece together the relationship between image and resource. This judgment once allowed the early investigation to move forward, but it is no longer suitable as a general explanation. It did not distinguish between "starting the investigation from this file" and "having confirmed where the relationships are resolved." The original wording is retained so that later readers can understand why the old record did not expand further, not to restore its status as a current conclusion.

## Two Approaches During Review

During the second round of editing, the real decision was not to invent a new policy for image, but to determine what judgments this page should allow. The file path is useful, but that does not mean it can carry implications beyond what the material supports.

**Continue treating a review of the file as the only place to check.** The advantage of this approach is the shortest lookup. The old record, issue names, call names, and `src/pages/background.js` can all point back to one another; someone opening the file for the first time can also immediately see `Log`, `T`, `ExtApi`, and `ExtMsg`. For someone who only needs to retrace the starting point of the old investigation, this information is practical enough.

The problem is that the names of direct dependencies are not evidence of policy. The presence of `ExtApi` or `ExtMsg` at the top of the file does not establish that image selection happens here; the visibility of `Log` and `T` does not establish that logging or utilities define resource priority either. More specifically, the current material does not prove that asset and image are necessarily evaluated in the same place, does not prove that source and attribute have a fixed precedence within this file, and does not prove that every resource on the browser side follows the same processing path. Including these unconfirmed relationships in the claim that this is the "only place to check" would misrepresent navigation clues as conclusions about behavior.

**Keep the file as the starting point for looking back, and leave policy verification to maintainers' routine checks.** This approach is somewhat slower, but it keeps the two tasks in their proper places. background.js continues to serve as the lookup entry point for old issues and the entry point for local declarations; during regression testing, maintainers check image capture policy using their routine procedure and record only the parts supported by actual material. Gaps for objects with no supporting evidence are not filled by relying on old call names.

v2 chose the latter approach. This decision does not discard the path or assert that the policy exists in some new module. Instead, it withdraws the inference that "the path itself is sufficient to make a policy judgment." For people who still rely on the old record, this change has a compatibility cost: they will continue to see v1's brief wording; removing that wording would make it impossible to explain why the early investigation started here. The old judgment therefore remains and is explicitly narrowed later on this page.

## After the Samples Were Added

MWC-206 later provided two verifiable actions: samples were attached on 2025-09-29, and the card moved from To Do to In Progress on 2025-10-02. These gave the review a concrete basis. The samples can be used to check image capture policy as part of maintainers' routine procedure, and they also mean that "leaving gaps where evidence is lacking" is no longer merely a way to avoid making a judgment.

But the card actions themselves did not provide a complete policy description. The samples are not evidence that background.js is authoritative, cannot by themselves confirm where the current value of resource. is obtained, cannot replace the choice between source and attribute, and cannot extend a local observation on the browser side to all resources. At one point, v2 tended toward "having samples is enough to continue making judgments based on the file"; the latest review narrowed this to "available samples can support regression testing within the scope of those samples." This distinction should be retained because the two statements lead to different scopes of documentation.

The samples also did not change the purpose of the original path. They did not make background.js lose its value: old issues still start here, and the four import statements at the top of the file remain visible clues to adjacent dependencies when reading. What changed is the threshold for writing down a conclusion. Paths, samples, actual references, and maintenance procedures are not the same kind of material, and none can substitute for all the others.

## The Boundaries Currently Retained

The decisions following the latest review are as follows.

1. Verification of image capture policy can start from `src/pages/background.js`. This file remains a historical lookup point, retaining the reading clues provided by its local declarations and direct dependencies.
2. The file path is no longer treated as the only place to check the image policy. `Log`, `T`, `ExtApi`, and `ExtMsg` are adjacency information, not proof that the relationships involving image, asset, source, attribute, browser, or resource. have been established.
3. Regression testing uses maintainers' routine checking procedure. The samples from MWC-206 can serve as material for this check; objects unsupported by material are explicitly left blank, and terms from the old investigation are not expanded into new behavioral commitments.
4. The old judgment from v1 remains on record, but is to be read only in its lookup context at the time. What has been withdrawn is the inference that "a complete policy can be obtained from background.js alone," not the value of this file as an entry point for looking back.

The state diagram below records only the checking sequence adopted on this page. It does not represent code execution flow or the specific selection algorithm for image:

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Entry
    state "background.js Entry Point for Looking Back" as Entry
    state "Maintainers' Routine Checks" as Review
    state "Check Within Sample Scope" as Sample
    state "Leave Unconfirmed Objects Blank" as Gap
    Entry --> Review
    Review --> Sample : Samples available
    Review --> Gap : Insufficient evidence
    Sample --> Gap : Cannot complete the relationships
    Gap --> [*]
```

The end state in the diagram does not mean that no other code relationships exist after checking stops. It means that this page no longer makes judgments about unconfirmed relationships. The available material only supports linking background.js, the samples, and the routine regression testing procedure into this chain of documentation. It does not support a specific selection algorithm for image, nor does it support incorporating policies for audio, video, or object here; even if they are all resource types, they cannot replace local verification of image.

## Traces of the Old Record Still on the Page

This material remains a history of the old entry point, not a new policy manual. The old investigation started from issue names and call names, and subsequent reviews have not overturned that fact. What was corrected later was its explanatory scope: starting from a searchable filename does not naturally establish that all resource decisions happen in the same place.

When further checking is needed, start from `src/pages/background.js` to examine local declarations and reference connections, then write back what can be confirmed by the samples and maintenance procedure. There is still not enough material on this page to confirm what the current value of resource. is, what the relationship between source and attribute is, or whether there are finer-grained branches on the browser side. Keeping these gaps is more useful than rephrasing the old judgment to make it look more like a current specification.

# Image source selection trial notes

The test sheet from May focused only on picture source selection. At the time, `src/js/capturer/picture.js` was treated as the first place to check, with the note, "Start by treating it as the only entry point for the selection logic." This was a provisional assumption to help with the investigation, not confirmed ownership.

Plan to save two sets of inputs: one that can complete capture, and one that fails after source selection. For both, copy down what actually remains on screen; if a resource task appears, also record source URL and whether the task continues on the same line. Seeing only that a task has started is not enough to show that the selected content made it into capture.

No failing sample was saved at the time. Next time, keep the same call context and change only the selected source. First add a record of what was visible in the successful call, then in the failed call. Question: did the failure come from no source being selected, or from the source being selected and then lost during subsequent resource processing?

# Image source selection trial notes

The May notes initially marked `src/js/capturer/picture.js` as the only place to check for picture source selection. That wording was only intended to give the capture investigation a starting point: look at the picture side first, then decide whether to follow the resource tasks further. The old wording is retained because it explains why the earliest samples only documented what happened up to around selection, and why the failed call wasn't saved separately.

This review withdraws the "only entry point" claim. The path still shows local declarations in the current revision and provides navigation to neighboring objects; but the file's location under capturer does not by itself show that source selection is implemented there, let alone establish ownership of subsequent resource processing. The old notes defined the starting point for verification too narrowly; it should no longer be treated as an implementation boundary.

The to-do item at MWC-210 requires two kinds of visible results to be saved: the existing user path supports picture source, and both a successful call and a failed call should have a record of what actually appeared on screen. The card did not include samples of these two calls. As a result, the successful call can only show that that particular capture left a result; it cannot be taken to mean that all sources have been covered. The failed call also cannot yet be directly attributed to no source having been selected.

Next round, keep the same call context as planned in May, changing only the selected source. Save the successful call's on-screen result first, then the failed call's on-screen result, to avoid putting the two observations in the same note. Each record must clearly identify the selected source; when a resource task appears, also copy down source URL, whether the task continues, and the order in which the on-screen result and the task appeared. A task having started is no substitute for the on-screen result, and an empty on-screen result does not, in turn, prove that no task was created.

Here, "failure after selection" is provisionally split into two unverified possibilities: the source was never selected, or it was selected but not retained during subsequent resource processing. Paired samples are needed to distinguish the two; the path's location cannot be used to choose an answer in advance.

This record does not include conclusions about current resource resolution. If the review finds that the source was selected but not retained on the resource side, continue the investigation at DOC-21; this page keeps only the inputs, actions, and visible observations for picture source selection.

```js
import {CSSRULE_TYPE} from '../lib/constants.js';

```

# Current Resource Resolution Decision Record

This record did not originally start from a named implementation branch. The old investigation left two leads: both the issue name and the call name led the reading to `src/js/snapshot/stylesheet.js`. What could be confirmed at the time was "there was a reasonable basis for starting the investigation here"; what could not be confirmed was "this was the responsibility point for current resource." These two judgments were kept separate throughout subsequent reviews.

First, record the original landing point. The path is located at `src/js/snapshot/stylesheet.js`, the repository index classifies it as an existing js module, and its local responsibility is described as "for code reading and checking historical behavior." It is the code entry point for the evolution of this request in Capture Pipeline 2.4, not a thumbnail of the entire capture pipeline. `capture boundary`, `frame ledger`, `resource task`, `source URL`, `asset cache`, and other project terms may belong to the same project, but no direct relationship with this path was established in the materials for this effort, so they were not included in this decision.

## First Page: Entry Point Before Ownership

The early judgment could easily be written as a stronger statement: "current resource resolution is handled in stylesheet.js." This sentence sounds smooth, but it simultaneously asserts the implementation location, resource-selection responsibility, and exception attribution. The original record provided only the issue name, call name, and file path, which could not support all three claims. Therefore, the first version labeled the file as an entry point, not as the fix point.

This was not merely conservative wording; it was the actual reading order used at the time. First, look within the file for the declarations and direct references of `stylesheet`, `document`, `resource`, `url`, and `link`; then confirm whether the imports at the top of the file are actually used; only when a new local reference appears should reading continue along that item. This preserves why the issue initially led us here, without miswriting the proximity between object names as a call relationship.

The first version also left a working hypothesis: the anomaly might be close to stylesheet-related snapshot processing. This hypothesis only sets priorities; it does not establish behavior. The counterexamples that could disprove it have clear forms: the issue name actually corresponds to a different file; `stylesheet.js` merely receives a value that has already been selected; the document or resource context has already been selected before reaching this file; or the actual use of `CssTextParser` and `CSSRULE_TYPE` leads the reading to another layer. That version had no references or action results for these counterexamples, so it neither revised its position prematurely nor presented the hypothesis as fact.

## The minimal evidence preserved in the file header

The file header's direct dependencies are recorded verbatim below:

```js
import T from '../lib/tool.js';
import ExtMsg from '../lib/ext-msg.js';
import {CSSRULE_TYPE} from '../lib/constants.js';
import CssTextParser from './css-text-parser.js';
```

These four lines serve different purposes in the history. First, they pin down the names that reviewers can see directly in the file header, preventing conjectured dependencies from being mixed in later; second, they provide an entry point for each possible direction of reading; finally, they preserve the granularity of the early record. They do not provide parameters, return values, or call order, so the main text does not fill in these details for any import.

`CSSRULE_TYPE` at least leads the reading back to local stylesheet-related code, but provides no enum members or branch conditions. `CssTextParser` makes parser a neighboring name that can be looked up, but there is no evidence that parser is responsible for current resource resolution. `ExtMsg` may connect the file to extension messaging, but the actual usage sites must still be the basis for judgment. `T` is likewise retained only as an import visible in the file header. Describing all these names as "the dependency modules are responsible for utilities, messaging, rules, and parsing, respectively" would go beyond the file-header facts provided in the input, so no such summary was made.

The file path itself also serves only for navigation. `snapshot` is a directory in the path, and `stylesheet.js` is the filename; the path does not indicate at which stage of the snapshot the processing occurs, nor whether the call occurs before or after resource selection. This history therefore records "adjacencies visible in the file header", rather than an end-to-end Capture Pipeline diagram.

## Three directions being compared

The review first needs to resolve an issue of semantic ordering: `current`, `resource`, and `resolution` appear next to one another in the requirements text, but adjacency does not make them the same thing. The record actually preserves three directions for reading.

| Line of inquiry | Local evidence to check | Reason for not adopting it upfront |
| --- | --- | --- |
| current is the resource already selected when stylesheet processing begins | How the value is passed in before entering the file, and whether it is only read within the file | The existing path and file header do not show how the value is passed in |
| current is re-derived during processing from the document or link context | References to `document`, `link`, and the term resource within the same local context | Object names alone cannot establish that the file controls selection |
| resolution refers to URL or path resolution, rather than resource selection | Where `url` is actually used and its relationship to the parser | Seeing `url` is not enough to prove that this is a path issue |

These three items are not three parallel proposals, nor are they three implementations of externally visible behavior. They are a way to break an ambiguous requirement down into observable questions. If the first item holds, stylesheet.js may simply be a downstream processing point; if the second item holds, the contextual relationships within the file need to be verified separately; if the third item holds, the requirement's focus would shift toward URL parsing rather than resource selection. The available input contains no cited passage or result that would allow a choice among them.

Therefore, the choice at the time was neither to "treat the file directly as the fix location" nor to "first combine stylesheet, document, and resource into a complete model". The actual decision was to retain the second working approach: start from the issue name, go into the file, check direct references, and then use those references to decide whether to expand the scope. This retains an extra layer of work compared with directly attributing a cause, but it does not fabricate callers or state changes in the historical record.

## What to actually examine during review

Review is not about stringing all project objects into a single chain. The first step is to look only at the declarations and local uses within `stylesheet.js`. If `stylesheet`, `document`, `resource`, `url`, or `link` appear only near message construction, record them together with that message's location; if they appear only near constant checks, retain the local context of those checks. The mere appearance of object terms cannot be taken as evidence that relationships between the objects have already been established.

The second step is to verify how the four imports are actually used. For `T`, check whether there are actual calls in the file; for `ExtMsg`, check whether it appears near message construction or publication; for `CSSRULE_TYPE`, check whether there are rule-type checks; for `CssTextParser`, check whether it is created or called directly by this file, or merely imported. Without these usage locations, we can only retain the names and entry points, not construct a seemingly complete execution sequence.

Only in the third step do we address the call name. The call name still points the issue to this file, but the path alone cannot tell us who the caller is, at which stage of snapshot the call occurs, whether resource selection has already been completed before the call, or whether the call leaves any visible changes. Here, "investigate further" means looking for local references, not assuming that an unseen call chain exists.

This is also why the requirements history did not include `resource task`, `source URL`, or `asset cache` in the current decision. They do appear in the project's vocabulary, but the materials frozen for this round did not establish any direct relationship between them and `stylesheet.js` through declarations, imports, or actions. Including them in the flow would only mistake the project's scope for evidence on this page.

## An earlier approach that was retained

At the time, one approach seemed to save effort: register the file pointed to by the issue name as the sole point of responsibility, and build all subsequent text around "stylesheet.js fixes current resource". Its advantage was brevity, and the entry point for investigation would not be lost; its disadvantage was that it turned navigation information into a judgment about the implementation. If it was later discovered that the caller was elsewhere, or that the file merely received predetermined values, the old record would be unable to explain why it had originally been written that way.

The second approach was to first build a complete model, linking stylesheet, document, resource, url, and link by name, and then go back to look for references. This approach was more complete than the first, but it treated the co-occurrence of terms as order and ownership. It would also naturally bring in neighboring objects such as `frame ledger`, `snapshot node`, and `shadow tree`, making this record appear to cover Capture Pipeline 2.4 without actually adding a single verifiable local fact.

The third approach was ultimately retained: use the file as the entry point, use direct imports for navigation, and list the still-unresolved relationships among the object terms as questions for review. This approach did not resolve the specific semantics of current resource resolution, but it accurately recorded the decision that could be made at the time. It also allowed later revisions to replace only the working hypothesis, without having to rewrite the file path and the recorded state of the file header.

## Boundary with stylesheet document base

`stylesheet document base` and this page both cover topics related to stylesheets, but they have separate long-term reference materials in the knowledge base. DOC-22 covers interface review; this page covers the requirements history and code entry points for current resource resolution. The two titles may share `stylesheet` or `document`, but that does not mean they made the same decision about the same relationship.

This boundary is especially important in the early stages. If the interface questions from DOC-22 are brought back here, this page will drift from "how the file entry point is determined" to "how the interface should be defined"; conversely, including this page's path entry points in the interface review would make file location look like an interface conclusion. In practice, only a single navigation reference is retained: when the adjacent interface topic is needed, go to DOC-22, without repeating its proposed approach, caller results, or compatibility assessments here.

Likewise, MWC-211 can provide a reproduction entry point for this page only after it appears, and cannot be used to rewrite the earlier draft. The observation recorded when the card was created was that current resource output could not be reproduced reliably; it moved the question from "whether the filename is relevant" to "whether the pre-call state and the visible changes after confirmation can be compared", but did not directly establish stylesheet.js as the point of attribution.

## The second stage introduced by the card

Later records about MWC-211 added a layer of practical work context to this history. Reproduction should start from the pre-call state, then check whether any additional visible changes remain after confirmation is complete. This entry point is more specific than looking only at the issue name, because it requires observing the states before and after confirmation within the same reproduction attempt; however, the card does not provide detailed results on reproduction success, failure, or state changes, so no results are added here.

In the action history for 2025-10-06, MWC-211 was marked as `failure_classified`. This indicates that the failure had entered the classification stage, but the action name did not specify what the classification was. It cannot be rewritten as "confirmed to be a stylesheet issue", nor can it be used to select any of the three semantic directions above. The action name is retained here to show when the requirements history moved from inconsistent reproduction into a handling stage that included classification.

On 2025-10-10, MWC-211 moved from To Do to In Progress and left `work_started`. This only indicates that actual work had begun; it cannot substitute for in-file references, a diff, or reproduction output. Nor did it change the earlier decision: the first code entry point remains `src/js/snapshot/stylesheet.js`, but the entry point still does not establish the cause of the failure.

The sequence of these two actions reveals a shift in understanding. The earliest question was "where to start looking"; after the card appeared, the question became "which pre-call state to reproduce from, and what additional changes to observe after confirmation"; classification and the start of work indicate that the work now had milestones marking its progress. The change was in the review entry point and the stage of work, not in implementation semantics. Without new local references, the action names cannot be used to fill in the relationships among document, resource, and url.

## Trade-offs retained after review

The review did not turn this page into a complete implementation description, but instead confirmed several trade-offs.

First, the path is retained as the initial reading entry point. This is based on the direction established during historical troubleshooting from the issue name and the call name; this does not make the path the sole point responsible for the issue.

Second, the four imports at the top of the file are retained as the minimal snapshot. Each appears under its original import name, making it easy to return to the top of the file and verify the adjacency visible at the time; their parameters, return values, and execution order are not filled in on this page.

Third, the meanings of `current`, `resource`, and `resolution` are not interchangeable. Only by examining local references can we determine whether this is processing a predetermined resource, reselecting within the context, or URL/path resolution.

Fourth, the reproduction entry point uses the scope retained from MWC-211: start from the pre-call state, and after confirming completion, observe whether there are any additional visible changes. The card's `failure_classified` and `work_started` are retained as traces of the stages, not treated as technical conclusions.

Fifth, stylesheet document base continues to be covered separately by DOC-22. Adjacent materials can link to each other for navigation, but the two decisions must not be merged simply because they share object terminology.

These choices preserve this page's role as a decision memo: it records the explanatory approaches that were compared, the attribution methods that were not adopted, and the review entry points that have been selected. It does not settle the final implementation semantics of current resource resolution; this is not an omitted summary, but the boundary of the decisions that the materials available at the time could support.

## Entry point and state evolution diagram

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Entry
    state "Issue name and call name point to stylesheet.js" as Entry
    state "Four direct imports at the top of the file" as Imports
    state "Review of declarations and direct references" as Review
    state "current/resource/resolution pending split" as Pending
    state "Reproduce from the pre-call state" as Repro
    state "failure_classified" as Classified
    state "work_started" as Started
    Entry --> Imports
    Imports --> Review
    Review --> Pending
    Review --> Repro
    Repro --> Classified
    Classified --> Started
```

"To be split" in the diagram is not a new state value, but rather the three avenues for review retained at the time: current may be a value that was already present when processing began, or it may relate to the document or link context; resolution may also refer to URL or path resolution. The diagram does not show any of these as confirmed behavior. `failure_classified` and `work_started` come from the historical actions in MWC-211, preserving the failure classification and the transition from To Do to In Progress, respectively.

## Current Local Decision

When returning to this path now, the first step is still not to map out the entire flow. First open `src/js/snapshot/stylesheet.js` and look at the object terms in the file and where the four imports are used; if the references show that a particular import does connect to the issue entry point, continue along that local relationship. If only a name is visible, with no usage, do not infer responsibilities for it.

Next, use the state before the call as the starting point for reproduction. What needs to be observed is whether any additional visible changes remain after confirmation is complete; attribution cannot be determined solely by whether the output contains terms such as `current resource`. The statement in MWC-211 that "current resource output cannot be reproduced consistently" is a starting point for review, not a fully explained failure case.

If new references prove that the issue name actually belongs to another file, revise the entry point hypothesis; if the references only prove that `stylesheet.js` receives a predetermined value, narrow the description of its responsibility; only if the references show that a new selection or resolution involving document, link or url occurs here should the corresponding avenue be included in the decision. All three cases require local references or action results and cannot be inferred solely from paths, import names or card status.

The only navigation targets still retained are this page's `src/js/snapshot/stylesheet.js`, the four imports at the top of the file, MWC-211 and the adjacent DOC-22. `internal/maoxian-core`'s `v_prev` is the repository and revision entry point for this source code reference; it helps locate the file viewed at the time, but does not mean that it provides unlisted implementation details. Going forward, if only a new path is available without references, update navigation at most, not attribution.

This is where this round of the decision history truly reaches closure: the first entry point has been selected, the lines of explanation that were compared have been preserved, the two rejected shorthand formulations have not been passed off as conclusions, and the reproduction details and stage changes provided by the cards have been linked in; as for the exact behavior of current resource resolution within the file, that still has to be determined through local references in that revision and actual verification.

# Stylesheet Document Base Plan

`src/js/snapshot/stylesheet.js` This entry point did not change between the two records. The adjacency visible in the file header is still `../lib/tool.js`, `../lib/ext-msg.js`, `CSSRULE_TYPE`, and `./css-text-parser.js`. These items constrain the verification scope to stylesheet objects, CSS rule classification, text parsing, and local tool/message dependencies; they do not identify the caller or directly explain where the stylesheet document base belongs. The earlier investigation pointed to this file from the issue name and call name. The current plan treats it only as a verification entry point and does not treat its path location as an implementation conclusion.

## Branches Left by the Initial Draft

The initial draft from 5 month only confirmed the shape of the problem. One direction was to use the stylesheet's fetched URL to resolve relative addresses in CSS text. The other was to pass document base, together with the containing document's context, through the reading, parsing, and serialization process. When the stylesheet's source address and the document base of the document using it happen to be the same, both directions may produce the same absolute address, so a single ordinary sample cannot prove that the choice is correct.

At the time, the correspondence among the input document, stylesheet source, CSS text, and parsed result was not recorded, and there were no parameter or return-value snippets for `CssTextParser`. As a result, the initial draft did not write `fetched`, `sheet`, and `values` as three definite fields of the same object; it treated them only as names to verify in local code. That limitation remains. v2 adds verification paths and trade-offs; it does not turn missing call results into conclusions.

The initial draft also compared "changing fewer parameters" with "preserving document semantics" without explaining what a rollback would affect. Now separate the two first: fetched URL records where the stylesheet was obtained, while document base records the document context in which the relative address exists. Their values may be the same, but at the plan level they cannot substitute for each other.

## Proposed Trial Shape

The first round should retain both the stylesheet's fetched URL and the document base of the document carrying it. Here, "retain" is a plan requirement, not a new field name; the actual field, parameter, or context member must be determined by the existing object shape of `stylesheet.js`. If an existing source object is available, first confirm that it can carry both semantics at once. If the interface has only one URL slot, record that limitation in the verification result instead of hiding the conflict by renaming it.

document base has three candidate consumption points:

1. Resolve relative addresses before passing CSS text to the parser. This lets the input carry the full context, but moves address handling earlier and may make the relationship between the raw text and its source unclear.
2. Pass base as the input context for `CssTextParser`. This lets the parser see the required information directly, but expands its responsibility beyond "text parsing," so first confirm that the existing interface actually accepts this kind of context.
3. Process it after the rules have been converted into `values`. This location requires fewer changes to the text parser, but may be too late if the conversion has already discarded the raw text or source.

For now, the more suitable shape to try is to retain the source explicitly at the higher layer and pass document base at the local location that actually consumes CSS values. This direction does not first override fetched URL, and it does not require `CssTextParser` to take on address resolution immediately. If verification shows that the parser already has the relevant input, then assess whether to continue passing the context into it. If it accepts only CSS text and produces structured results, base can remain at the call site or in the higher-level object. Both outcomes should be retained; do not preemptively classify the parser as the final responsible party.

A path without document base should not currently borrow fetched URL as a fill value. It has not yet been decided whether the missing value should preserve the relative content, skip subsequent value retrieval, or be handed to the higher layer. Silently treating fetched URL as the default will make ordinary samples look normal, but will not distinguish the role of the source address from that of the containing document.

## How to Perform Local Verification

Verification starts at the locations inside `src/js/snapshot/stylesheet.js` that actually create parser input and handle `sheet`, `fetched`, and `values`. First record one set of input document, stylesheet source, raw CSS, and serialized result, then mark whether document base exists. The focus is not merely comparing the final absolute address, but confirming where base is consumed and whether the original source remains visible after serialization.

The samples must form at least two distinguishable sources: fetched URL differs from document base; another set lacks document base. The first set is used to observe whether the two values are retained separately, and the second to observe whether the system silently borrows fetched URL. If the existing interface cannot construct these two inputs, record the construction limitation first; do not equate failure to construct them with plan failure.

Add a CSS text with no relative address as a control. It can confirm that document base does not cause unrelated address rewriting when there is no relative content. If the same stylesheet can be reused in different document contexts, also check one reuse path to see whether base remains from the previous processing; the current material does not prove that this path exists, so perform this only when it is actually visible in the file.

Keep the recorded items within local-object scope:

| Location | Content to retain | Question to answer |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Input | document, stylesheet source, CSS text | Are both sources visible at the same time? |
| Before and after parsing | The parser's actual input and `values` | Does base take effect before the text, during parsing, or after conversion? |
| Serialization | Original content and serialized content | Is the source lost, or is the relative address rewritten? |
| Missing context | Result without document base | Is the behavior to retain, skip, or pass upward? |

The items in the table define the shape of the verification record; they are not checks that have already passed. The frozen material provides no specific commands, selectors, page addresses, or output values, so this plan does not invent reproducible examples. If existing tests or examples are needed to trigger stylesheet document base, the related to-do remains recorded by `MWC-212`, but that card had not yet reached a citable state when the two versions were written; this page does not backfill it into the historical body. When there is an adjacent relationship with local run records for CSS selector text, navigation can go through `DOC-23`, but it must not be used to fill in this page's test results.

## Trade-offs of the Candidate Plans

**Use only fetched URL.** This is the minimal-change direction. It may preserve the observable results of existing ordinary paths and can continue to represent where the stylesheet was obtained. However, when the stylesheet is used in another document context, it has no place to express the second address semantic; if an incorrect result appears later, it will be impossible to tell whether the source selection was wrong or the parsing stage used the wrong context. This direction can serve only as a comparison and should not be finalized directly.

**Use only document base.** This directly expresses the document carrying the relative address, but makes the original stylesheet source invisible. If it is later necessary to investigate where the stylesheet was obtained, or whether it went through serialization or reuse, a single base will force both questions into one value. This direction is closer to document semantics than the first, but is not suitable as the only source record.

**Keep both, with the local consumption point explaining their uses.** This direction increases the cost of constructing inputs, passing data, and creating test samples, and requires every path that can provide document context to confirm the parameter shape. Its benefit is that the source and containing context will not overwrite each other at the entry point, and the verification result can also show which location consumed base. The current recommendation is to try this shape, but not to write it as the final interface that has already been decided.

The consumption position of base must also be compared separately. Rewriting CSS text in advance makes absolute addresses available to downstream consumers, but may erase the original content; letting the parser consume the context can centralize handling, but changes the responsibility of `CssTextParser`; waiting until `values` has been formed before processing touches text parsing less, but may lose source information. The choice should be determined by the actual parameters, return values, and serialization behavior, not by filenames or dependency names.

## Points Not Resolved in Review

It has not yet been decided whether document base is a separate context value, part of the existing stylesheet object, or temporarily provided by the call site. It has also not been decided whether a missing base should preserve the relative value, skip continued value retrieval, or hand the gap to the higher layer. The three missing-base behaviors have different downstream costs: preserving the current state may prevent downstream resource creation, skipping may produce an empty result, and handing it to the higher layer requires confirming that a receiving position actually exists. The existing material contains no choice, logs, or caller convention, so this page retains only the disagreement.

The responsibility of `CssTextParser` is also undecided. The file header can confirm only that it is a direct dependency; it cannot show that it already accepts document base or that it is responsible for address resolution. If verification shows that the parser only consumes CSS text and produces structured results, the plan should avoid expanding the parser just to pass context. If it already has related inputs, then assess placing base in its input context. Neither outcome should be substituted by `CSSRULE_TYPE`, because rule classification and document address have different semantics.

`../lib/tool.js` and `../lib/ext-msg.js` are currently retained only as file adjacency. There is no material showing that the tool layer or message layer already carries the base selection, and no material showing that this trial requires new error wording. If verification produces failure output, record the raw input, failure location, and result; do not automatically promote the message dependency into a new interface responsibility.

## When to Roll Back

If the local trial must override fetched URL to continue working, first roll back the newly added base propagation and do not extend the overwritten value to other rule processing. If the parser's input shape would make the original CSS disappear, stop at the parser boundary and retain the observation that the sources are separate. If only the old path without document context cannot continue, roll back only the new propagation for that path; do not silently fill it with another URL.

Limit the rollback scope to newly added parameter passing or local consumption positions. Do not delete fetched URL, and do not replace the original CSS with a serialized address; otherwise, the next round will not be able to distinguish source loss, parse failure, and serialization rewriting. There is no evidence that `CSSRULE_TYPE`, the tool dependency, the message dependency, and the existing text-parsing relationship need to be rolled back together.

## Interim Position Before Verification Is Complete

This plan can enter a small-scope interface review, but it cannot serve as the complete stylesheet convention for Capture Pipeline 2.4. First confirm how the existing objects in `stylesheet.js` carry the source, trace the parser's actual input and output along the visible adjacency, and then use samples with different sources and missing base to distinguish the candidate directions. If the review still cannot determine the consumption position, retain the unresolved items and do not expand a guess into a global rule.

# CSS Selector Text Troubleshooting Tree

This page still comes up under the old issue name, so it retains the original, very narrow path: `src/js/snapshot/css-text-parser.js`. It was originally a place to investigate CSS selector text, not an explanation of the entire Capture Pipeline, and the path alone cannot establish implementation ownership.

The initial notes contained a convenient but overly strong assumption: the issue name contained CSS, and the filename also contained css-text, so the difference was initially attributed to this location. That assumption helped people open the right directory, but conflated "finding a file that might process the text" with "confirming that the text was changed here". Subsequent reviews had no material supporting the latter claim; the old assumption has not been deleted, but it is no longer used as a basis for changes.

## Start with the text at hand

A reported selector text anomaly should at least identify an actual piece of text, or its location in a snapshot result. Descriptions such as "the styling is gone" or "the selector changed" can remain in the incident notes, but are not sufficient to move directly to file inspection: the former describes the observed page appearance, while the latter could also be a difference that was already present at an earlier point.

First distinguish where the text came from. Characters seen on the page, characters in the snapshot, and characters copied from subsequent output must not be treated as the same input just because they look similar. Whenever a piece of text appears in the notes, label its source; if uncertain, write "location unconfirmed" rather than prematurely calling it parser output.

```text
Observed CSS selector text does not match expectations
|
+-- Can the original selector text be provided?
|   |
|   +-- No: record the page or snapshot location and the observed result; stop attributing a cause
|   |
|   `-- Yes: save the text as is, without replacing whitespace, quotation marks, or suspicious fragments
|
+-- Can the location of another comparable piece of text be identified?
|   |
|   +-- No: record the "text form" and "snapshot location" separately
|   |
|   `-- Yes: compare character differences and their respective locations
|
`-- Does the report explicitly mention style scope rewriting?
    |
    +-- Yes: save the two descriptions separately, and consult DOC-24 if needed
    |
    `-- No: stay on the CSS selector text branch
```

"Stop" in the tree does not mean that the symptom has disappeared, but that the current material is insufficient to locate the difference at a particular processing point. Previous investigations often continued outward from here to trace resources, nodes, or saved results, only to end up without a comparable selector. When moving away from CSS text, first save the current text and its location, then hand off to a separate record.

## Compare only the two known endpoints

When two pieces of text are available, compare the characters themselves first. Do not start by discussing whether the two selectors are equivalent, or use page behavior as a substitute for character differences. If one piece of text appears in style-related content and the other in a snapshot fragment, the notes must specify that distinction; they are not inherently "before processing" and "after processing".

If the texts really are different, return to `src/js/snapshot/css-text-parser.js` and look at the processing near the current text. The goal here is to find a local point that can explain how the text enters, is split, or is reassembled, rather than reading through the entire snapshot directory. When excerpting nearby content, make sure later readers can tell whether the section is receiving text, reading text, or generating another piece of text. Without a sample from the incident, branches in the file are only candidate locations.

If the difference is already visible before the text enters this file, stop on the side of the earlier entry point. The old notes loosely called this an "upstream issue", which introduced an unnecessary implication: it sounds as though the earlier entity is already known. A safer way to record it is that the current comparison shows the difference appearing before the local processing point, but where it formed has not yet been confirmed.

If the two texts are identical, and their respective locations offer no clues establishing a replacement relationship, the page anomaly must no longer be recorded as a selector text change. An early side note recommended continuing to look for conditional branches around the parser; that recommendation had no corresponding text difference, so it is now retained as a past attempt, not as the next step.

## Shortcuts taken in the past

Old reports often contained only a screenshot, or only said that a selector with a suspected scope-related fragment had been seen. Investigators would first remove the fragment, then check whether the page returned to normal. # Caller Integration Test Routing Proposal

For integration testing, we first narrowed the debate to one question: should the existing `asset cache` continue to handle caller integration, or should `snapshot node` be split out on its own? At the time, this proposal leaned toward the latter—not because the two had different names, but because the two recorded failure exits didn't look like the same kind of failure.

The materials are temporarily stored at `docs/adj-js/proposals/not-adopted-js-caller-integration-approach.md`. They divide the failure exits into a cache path and a node path; as understood at the time, the former could continue through the existing caller flow, while the latter should have its own integration surface. If we keep forcing them into the same path, callers can only see "no content retrieved," without being able to tell whether it was a cache miss or the node itself left no usable result.

The proposed trial change is small: keep the existing entry point for `asset cache` and do not replace it in this round; the newly created `snapshot node` would only accept content that needs to be saved separately. Callers would first choose based on the existing branches, still falling back to the old entry point when they can't decide. The benefit is that existing callers wouldn't all need to be updated at once, and the download side could inspect failure exits independently. The cost is that both paths would coexist for a while, so any investigation must start by asking which path the caller actually took.

There was no agreement at the time to split out `stylesheet base` as well. Not all of its active callers had been identified yet. If it were bundled into the same trial as `snapshot node`, a failure would make it hard to tell whether the style baseline changed the result or the new node's save logic had a problem. The tentative position here is to leave `stylesheet base` in place; consider moving it only after confirming that existing callers no longer use it directly.

The objections to continuing along `asset cache` were also limited in scope. The cache route is suited to repeated reads by existing callers, but it uses the same framing for the saved object and the read result. For this integration test, the view was that `snapshot node` needed to save its own object first, then let callers decide whether to read it. This distinction has not yet been made an interface constraint; treat it as an assumption for the trial.

The plan for the trial window is to add a contrasting input: send the same caller through the old cache route and the new node route separately, focusing on whether `download path` can still identify the branch actually taken. If the failure exits the two routes ultimately produce are no different, or the new node must depend on the old entry point to complete the save, roll back the split and restore only the old entry point, without also addressing `stylesheet base`.

Open questions:

- Which callers currently use `stylesheet base`;
- Whether the scope of the contrasting input is sufficient to cover the download side;
- Whether the `snapshot node` objects already written need to be retained after rollback;
- Where the caller selection criteria are specified while both routes coexist.

This is therefore not a proposal to replace `asset cache`, but to first take `snapshot node` out of the shared caller path for a trial. There is no start time, and the trial is not being treated as a change already in effect.

When the current entry point gets stuck, first leave the page at the point where the symptoms are visible. The old tree only routes the case to `pages-quality-signal`, the exit action, or the permissions owner; it is not a substitute for recovery actions and does not turn nodes without evidence into a final cause.

This tree was written for the page state at that time. If the entry point no longer shows its original display, or only a retelling remains, do not guess down the tree. Retain the minimal input that reproduces the hang and the current page, then decide whether to continue.

## First check whether the tree is still there

1. Open `docs/adj-pages/runbooks/pages-quality-signal-who-to-contact-when-stuck.md` and look for `shadow tree`.
2. If you can't find the tree, stay at the entry point. Do not switch to `pages-quality-signal` just because the names are similar.
3. Once you find the tree, select only the branch matching the symptom in front of you. If the preceding branch has no evidence, do not jump to the terminal handler.

"Evidence" is narrowly defined here: a state still visible on the page, retained input, or a node already present in the tree. An inference beyond the logs does not count as a reason to cross a branch.

- The tree has already shown `document base`: preserve the state; do not clean up. In the old record, this node means you can continue down the tree, but it does not yet establish that collection or execution has occurred.
